items.title: Bluetooth/BLE Coexistence Attacks
items.prerequisites: A Bluetooth/BLE-capable adapter with monitor/sniffing support (e.g. Ubertooth One, or an nRF52-based sniffer for BLE). Tooling such as InternalBlue, the KNOB/BIAS proof-of-concept scripts, or Wireshark with a Bluetooth capture. Written authorization covering Bluetooth/BLE interception testing, distinct from the Wi-Fi authorization since this targets a different radio and protocol stack.
items.whatItIs: WiFi and Bluetooth often share the same radio chip, and a few real vulnerabilities (KNOB, BLURtooth, and similar) let an attacker weaken the encryption negotiated during Bluetooth pairing, or exploit shared trust between the two radios on the same chip. KNOB specifically lets an attacker force the Bluetooth session's encryption key down to as little as a single byte — small enough to brute-force in seconds.
items.rootCause: Classic Bluetooth lets two devices agree on how strong their encryption key should be — but that negotiation itself isn't protected. An attacker sitting in the middle can quietly rewrite that agreement down to the weakest option, and neither device notices. On chips where WiFi and Bluetooth share more than just hardware — like session keys or trust state — breaking into one radio's security can spill over into the other.
items.impact: Once the key length is forced down, the attacker brute-forces the session key in real time and can then decrypt or inject into the Bluetooth session. Depending on what is paired, that extends to keyboards, headsets, and medical or industrial devices. Where the chip bridges trust between its radios, it can also provide a pivot onto the co-located Wi-Fi radio's state.
stepsToIdentify: Inventory Bluetooth/BLE-capable devices in scope and check chipset/firmware versions against the published KNOB and BLURtooth advisory lists.
With authorization, monitor a pairing/reconnection event between two test devices and inspect the negotiated encryption key length for evidence of downgrade susceptibility.
Check whether affected devices have received the vendor firmware patches addressing KNOB (most major stacks patched by 2020) and BLURtooth (2020 disclosure, Bluetooth 4.0-5.0 affected).
Assess what's reachable or controllable via the paired BLE peripheral if the session is compromised (e.g. a smart lock, industrial sensor, or wireless keyboard) to size real-world impact.
Inventory which Bluetooth and BLE devices share a radio with the wireless adapter, since combo chipsets arbitrate between the two and a saturated Bluetooth channel degrades Wi-Fi on the same device.

Confirm whether any security control depends on a Bluetooth link — a proximity unlock, a wireless barcode scanner, a medical telemetry link — because those are the assets a coexistence attack actually reaches.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes active Bluetooth/BLE key-negotiation manipulation against nominated test devices.
Position as an on-path observer/relay during a pairing or reconnection event between two test devices.
Intercept and rewrite the encryption key length negotiation to the minimum permitted value before the devices complete pairing.
Brute-force the resulting low-entropy session key in real time and demonstrate decryption or injection into the session as proof of concept.
Where coexistence/BLURtooth conditions are also being tested, attempt to demonstrate any trust bridging into the co-located Wi-Fi radio's state, strictly against nominated test hardware.

KNOB proof-of-concept key-length downgrade (research toolkit, authorized lab use only)
Inspect negotiated key length in a capture
examplePayloads.command: tshark -r capture.pcap -Y 'btl2cap or bthci_evt' -V | grep -i 'key size\|entropy'

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate BLE devices advertising in range along with their addresses and RSSI
examplePayloads.command: sudo btmgmt find || sudo hcitool lescan --duplicates

examplePayloads.label: Confirm channel overlap between the active Wi-Fi channel and observed Bluetooth activity
examplePayloads.command: iw dev wlan0 info && sudo btmon | grep -i 'channel'

variants: BLURtooth cross-transport key derivation abuse, where a compromised BLE session key is used to derive or overwrite the classic BR/EDR key (or vice versa) on dual-mode devices.
Coexistence-firmware trust bridging specific to combo Wi-Fi/Bluetooth chipsets, where shared firmware state allows a compromise on one radio to weaken the other.
BLE advertisement flooding, which saturates the scanning window of nearby devices and prevents a legitimate peripheral being discovered or reconnecting.
Deliberate 2.4 GHz coexistence pressure on a combo chipset, degrading the Wi-Fi link on a target device without transmitting any 802.11 frame that a wireless IDS would record.
mitigation: Apply vendor firmware/OS patches addressing KNOB (CVE-2019-9506) and BLURtooth (CVE-2020-15802 and related) across all Bluetooth/BLE-capable devices.
Where firmware allows, enforce a minimum acceptable encryption key length (16 bytes) and reject connections that negotiate below it, rather than accepting whatever the peer proposes.
Disable Bluetooth/BLE entirely on devices that don't require it, reducing the attack surface regardless of patch status.
For high-security environments, treat combo Wi-Fi/Bluetooth chipsets as a single trust boundary during risk assessment rather than assuming the two radios are independently secured.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Bluetooth and Wi-Fi share the same radio space and, on most devices, the same chip. That means Bluetooth activity nearby can degrade or interrupt a device's wireless connection without a single wireless frame being sent, so nothing appears in your wireless monitoring. This matters where something you depend on runs over Bluetooth — a proximity unlock, a scanner, a headset, telemetry equipment. Identify those dependencies first, since they determine whether this is a minor issue or an operational one, and make sure anything critical has a fallback that does not rely on either radio.

items.title: Captive Portal Bypass
items.prerequisites: A device capable of associating to the target open/captive-portal network. A general-purpose OS with the ability to modify its MAC address and inspect/craft DNS and HTTP requests. Written authorization to bypass the portal's access control for testing purposes.
items.whatItIs: Captive portals (the 'log in to use this WiFi' page) work by having the network's equipment track which device has completed the login step, and block everyone else. Since that tracking is usually based only on the device's address (which is easy to fake) and since DNS traffic is often left wide open so the portal itself can work, there are several well-known ways to reach the internet — or, on poorly segmented networks, internal systems — without ever actually logging in.
items.rootCause: The portal decides whether you're 'logged in' based on things that are either easy to fake (your device's address) or left deliberately open as a side channel (DNS), instead of something cryptographically tied to an actual completed login. Wherever DNS is left unfiltered so the portal page itself can load, that same open channel becomes a way to sneak other traffic through, disguised as DNS lookups.
items.impact: The attacker gets free network access, bypassing whatever billing, terms-of-service or identity-tracking purpose the portal existed to serve. Where DNS tunnelling is the route in, there is a second consequence: a low-bandwidth but working channel for data exfiltration or command and control. That channel survives on networks which otherwise correctly block every other kind of pre-login traffic.
stepsToIdentify: Associate to the target open/captive-portal SSID without completing the login/acceptance step and probe whether any traffic (DNS, ICMP, specific TCP/UDP ports) is passed through before authentication.
If DNS resolution succeeds pre-authentication, test whether arbitrary data can be tunneled through DNS queries/responses (a strong indicator of a viable bypass channel).
Identify a MAC address already authenticated on the network (from a legitimately connected device, observed passively) and attempt MAC spoofing to inherit its authenticated session.
Check whether the portal's enforcement is IP-based only, in which case simply configuring a static IP within the authenticated range (if guessable/known) may grant access without any MAC spoofing.

Test whether HTTPS destinations are blocked pre-authentication the same as HTTP, since some portal implementations only intercept/redirect port 80 and leave 443 traffic to fail open or pass through unfiltered.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes captive-portal bypass testing.
Associate to the portal-protected SSID and, before completing login, attempt DNS resolution of an arbitrary external domain to check whether it succeeds.
If DNS is open, set up a DNS tunneling client/server pair (e.g. iodine or dnscat2) and demonstrate a working data channel through the unauthenticated portal state.

Separately, passively observe an already-authenticated client's MAC address, then spoof it on a second test device to check whether the network grants access based on MAC alone without re-prompting for authentication.
Where a static-IP bypass is suspected, manually configure an IP address within the observed authenticated range and confirm whether traffic is permitted.
Document which specific technique succeeded and the exact scope of access obtained (internet-only vs. any internal reachability) for the report.

examplePayloads.label: Test pre-authentication DNS resolution
DNS tunneling proof-of-concept through an open pre-auth DNS channel
Spoof an observed, already-authenticated client MAC
examplePayloads.command: ip link set wlan0 down && macchanger -m <observed-authenticated-mac> wlan0 && ip link set wlan0 up

examplePayloads.label: Attempt static-IP bypass within the authenticated range

variants: HTTPS-only fail-open, where only port 80 is intercepted by the portal and port 443 traffic passes through unauthenticated entirely.
Session-cookie replay, where a captured portal session token is replayed from a different device/MAC to inherit authentication.
MAC address cloning of an already-authorised session, where the portal treats the address as the session identity and a second device inherits the authenticated state.
Pre-authentication DNS or ICMP tunnelling, which carries traffic through the resolver the portal must leave open before any payment or acceptance step has completed.
mitigation: Block all traffic (including DNS) other than what's strictly required to reach the portal itself until authentication/acceptance is complete, closing the DNS-tunneling side channel.

Bind portal sessions to a combination of factors harder to spoof than MAC/IP alone (e.g. 802.1X-based identity where feasible, or short-lived cryptographically signed session tokens tied to the specific connection).
Ensure HTTP and HTTPS destinations are enforced identically pre-authentication rather than only intercepting port 80.
Rate-limit and monitor for rapid MAC-address changes or duplicate-MAC association attempts, which are strong indicators of an in-progress bypass attempt.
Periodically re-test the portal after any controller/firmware upgrade, since bypass regressions are common when vendors update their captive-portal implementation.
items.mitigationClientFacing: The sign-in page on your guest network can be bypassed, so a visitor can use the connection without ever accepting the terms or being recorded. That undermines the acceptable-use agreement and the visitor record that the portal exists to produce, which may matter more for your obligations than for security. Some bypass methods are inherent to how these portals work and cannot be fully closed. The practical position is to stop treating the portal as a security control, ensure the guest network is properly separated from everything internal regardless of who is on it, and keep the portal for the terms acceptance and logging it genuinely does provide.

items.title: Evil Twin / Rogue Access Point
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and packet injection. hostapd (standard, not necessarily Karma mode) configured to clone a specific known SSID, plus a means to run a stronger signal than the legitimate AP. Written authorization for active rogue-AP deployment against a specific, named corporate SSID.
items.whatItIs: An Evil Twin is a deliberate copy of one specific, real network name the organisation actually uses. It is set up to trick devices that already trust that name into connecting to the attacker instead of the genuine access point, usually by presenting a stronger signal or by first kicking devices off the real one. This differs from a Karma attack, which impersonates whatever network a device happens to be searching for.
items.rootCause: Just like with Karma, a device decides to connect based on the network's name matching one it trusts — there's no real proof the AP answering is the genuine one. For open or basic password-protected networks, there's nothing distinguishing the real access point from a copy, beyond a technical ID number almost no one ever checks.
items.impact: Employees and visitors connect believing they are on the legitimate network, which hands the attacker a transparent interception position over all their traffic. From there they can phish credentials through a spoofed captive portal, attempt to downgrade encrypted connections, and inject content into any unencrypted session. This is the foundational technique behind most real-world rogue access point incidents, and it is usually paired with the DNS and deauthentication findings recorded separately.
stepsToIdentify: Establish a baseline inventory of legitimate BSSIDs for every corporate SSID (from the wireless controller) and periodically scan for any additional AP broadcasting the same SSID from an unrecognized BSSID.
Compare signal strength and channel of any suspect duplicate against the legitimate AP's documented deployment to assess how competitive the rogue AP would be for real client association.

Check whether the security type advertised by the duplicate matches the legitimate network exactly (an Evil Twin cloning an open network is far easier to pull off convincingly than one attempting to clone WPA2-Enterprise, see the related EAP-specific finding).
Confirm whether WIDS/WIPS is deployed and correctly alerting on unauthorized BSSIDs broadcasting known corporate SSIDs.

Compare the BSSID and vendor OUI of every AP advertising the corporate SSID against the controller's own inventory, since a rogue is identified by the address behind the name rather than the name itself.

Check whether client devices are configured to require a specific server certificate for the corporate SSID, because a client that validates the certificate will not complete authentication against a twin.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorizes active Evil Twin deployment against a named corporate SSID and, where real bystander devices may associate, the handling process for that traffic.
Configure hostapd to broadcast the exact target SSID and matching security type (open/WPA2-Personal) from a position with strong signal relative to the legitimate AP.
Where needed to accelerate association, deauthenticate a nominated test client from the legitimate AP so it searches for and finds the rogue AP.
Confirm association of the (test or, where explicitly authorized, any) client and demonstrate MITM impact — DNS/HTTP interception, or a spoofed portal login capture — as proof of concept.
Tear down the rogue AP immediately once the finding is proven and confirm no real, non-test traffic was retained beyond what's needed as evidence.

Force a nominated test client to search for alternatives
Confirm client association to the rogue AP

variants: Signal-strength-only Evil Twin relying purely on physical positioning rather than active deauthentication to win the association race.
Evil Twin combined with a spoofed captive portal for credential harvesting (overlaps with the rogue-DNS/captive-portal finding).
A rogue AP plugged into a live corporate access port, which bridges the wireless attacker directly onto the internal network rather than merely intercepting traffic.
An evil twin standing up only outside working hours, which evades a survey conducted during the day and is the common shape when the operator has periodic physical access.
mitigation: Deploy WIDS/WIPS with rogue-AP detection tuned to alert on any BSSID broadcasting a known corporate SSID that isn't in the authorized inventory.
Require WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with certificate validation so an Evil Twin cannot present valid credentials to a client that correctly validates the RADIUS server certificate.
Enable 802.11w/PMF to reduce the effectiveness of the deauthentication-based association-forcing technique.
Educate users to check for consistent, expected certificate/portal behavior and to report unexpected reconnection prompts or repeated login requests.
Physically survey for unauthorized APs periodically, especially near high-traffic areas (lobbies, meeting rooms) where a rogue AP is easy to plant discreetly.
items.mitigationClientFacing: An attacker can broadcast a network with the same name as yours, and devices in range will join it, believing it is the real one. Everything those devices then send passes through equipment the attacker controls. The reason this works is that your devices check the name but not the identity behind it. Configure managed devices to verify the network's certificate before connecting, which makes an imitation fail outright. Separately, enable rogue detection on your wireless controllers, because at present a copy of your network could operate indefinitely without anyone knowing — and the same detection catches an unauthorised access point plugged in by a well-meaning employee.

items.title: Insecure Wi-Fi Direct Pairing
items.prerequisites: Two Wi-Fi Direct-capable devices (or one attacker device plus a target), and packet-capture/injection tooling capable of monitoring the Wi-Fi Direct (P2P) discovery and pairing exchange. Written authorization to test pairing against a nominated target device.
items.whatItIs: Wi-Fi Direct lets two devices connect to each other directly without a router in between, using either a PIN or a simple button-press to pair. Several implementations have been found using predictable or even fixed PINs, accepting a replayed old pairing attempt without asking again, or falling back to a weaker pairing method when the stronger one isn't available on both sides — any of which lets an attacker pair with a device, or pretend to be one it already trusts, without real consent.
items.rootCause: Wi-Fi Direct's pairing methods borrow a lot from an older, already-broken system (WPS), including small or predictable PINs, and it allows both sides to fall back to whichever method they both support — which an attacker can exploit by simply pretending to only support the weakest one available.
items.impact: Unauthorised pairing allows direct file transfer to the target device, hijacking of screen mirroring, or use of the peer connection as a pivot into whatever network access that device already holds. The legitimate user never consented to that specific pairing session, and in most cases has no clear indication it happened.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate Wi-Fi Direct-capable/discoverable devices in scope and record their advertised provisioning methods (PIN, push-button, NFC) from the P2P discovery frames.
With authorization, attempt PIN-based pairing against a nominated test device and check whether the PIN is fixed, predictable, or brute-forceable within a reasonable attempt budget.
Test whether a previously-captured pairing exchange can be replayed to re-establish a connection without fresh user interaction on the target device.
Check whether the device correctly requires explicit, per-session user confirmation (a visible prompt) for push-button pairing, or whether it silently auto-accepts under certain conditions.
Determine which Wi-Fi Direct pairing method each device negotiates, since push-button pairing authenticates nobody and PIN-based pairing inherits the WPS weaknesses covered separately.
Establish whether Wi-Fi Direct remains enabled on printers and displays outside their provisioning window, because most are configured once and left advertising permanently.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active Wi-Fi Direct pairing attempts against the nominated test device.
Capture the P2P discovery/negotiation exchange to identify the provisioning method(s) the target device will accept.
Attempt PIN brute-force or use of a previously-known default/predictable PIN for that vendor/model.
Where a captured prior pairing exchange is available, attempt to replay it to reconnect without fresh user confirmation.
Demonstrate impact via a benign action on the paired connection (file transfer of a test artifact, screen-mirror connection) rather than exfiltrating real data from the target device.

variants: Push-button auto-accept misconfiguration, where the device pairs without a genuine user confirmation prompt under specific state conditions (e.g. screen already unlocked and app in foreground).
NFC-triggered pairing bypass, relevant only on devices that support NFC-initiated Wi-Fi Direct handoff.
A persistent Wi-Fi Direct group that re-forms automatically after a reboot, so a single successful pairing survives the maintenance window that was expected to clear it.
A device bridging its Wi-Fi Direct group to the corporate WLAN it is also joined to, which turns an unauthenticated peer link into a path onto the production network.
mitigation: Disable Wi-Fi Direct on managed devices where the business use case doesn't require it.
Where Wi-Fi Direct is required, prefer push-button configuration with mandatory, visible per-session user confirmation over PIN-based pairing.
Keep device OS/firmware current, since PIN predictability and replay-acceptance issues are typically vendor-specific bugs addressed via patches.
For high-security environments, use MDM policy to block P2P/Wi-Fi Direct connections entirely at the OS level.

items.title: Insecure Wireless Printer Direct Connection
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter within range of the target printer's direct/AP-mode Wi-Fi interface. Basic network scanning tools (nmap) and a printer-protocol client (IPP/LPD/raw port 9100). Written authorization to interact with the discovered printer interface.
items.whatItIs: A lot of wireless printers offer a direct-connect mode so people can print without joining the main corporate network — but this mode often ships with no password, a fixed default password, or an admin panel still using default login details. And since the printer is usually also plugged into the wired network, this 'convenience' feature can become an unguarded doorway straight into the internal network.
items.rootCause: The direct-connect feature is meant to be easy to use without needing corporate credentials — but that convenience is often left exactly as it shipped, with default (or no) authentication, and with no separation between that direct-connect interface and the printer's normal wired network connection.
items.impact: An attacker in range gains an unauthenticated foothold. Where the printer bridges its wireless and wired interfaces, that foothold reaches the internal network the printer sits on, bypassing corporate Wi-Fi authentication entirely. Even with no bridge, they can intercept or inject print jobs and read the device's stored job history, which frequently contains sensitive scanned or printed documents.
stepsToIdentify: Survey for printer-vendor SSIDs (commonly named after the make/model, e.g. "DIRECT-xx-HP...") in scope and note their advertised security type.
Attempt association using default/no passphrase for the identified vendor/model.
Once associated, scan for reachability into the printer's wired-side network to confirm whether the direct-connect interface is bridged rather than isolated.
Check the printer's admin web interface (if reachable) for default credentials.
Review job-history/stored-document retention settings on the device, since accessible print queues can themselves be a data-exposure finding independent of network bridging.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes interaction with the discovered printer interface and any onward network access it exposes.
Associate to the printer's direct-connect SSID using default/no passphrase.
Attempt to reach the printer's admin interface and, where default credentials work, confirm access without altering configuration.
Test onward network reachability from the printer's IP to representative internal hosts to determine whether the direct-connect segment is bridged to the wired network.
Where reachable, submit a benign test print job to confirm functional access, and check for accessible stored job history as a secondary data-exposure finding.
Document the exact bridging behavior observed, since remediation priority differs sharply between an isolated direct-connect interface and one that bridges onto the internal network.

Scan the printer's IP once associated
Attempt raw-port print-queue interaction
Check onward reachability into the wired network

variants: Print-job interception/injection on the raw JetDirect (port 9100) protocol, which carries no authentication or encryption by default.
Stored scan/job-history exposure via an unauthenticated web interface, independent of any network-bridging concern.
The printer's embedded web server reachable over its direct link with default or absent credentials, exposing stored scan destinations and address-book entries.
Stored print jobs retrievable from the device over the direct link, which discloses document content without any access to the corporate network.
mitigation: Disable Wi-Fi Direct/AP-mode printing where not operationally required, or set a strong, unique passphrase where it is.
Ensure the printer's direct-connect interface is not bridged to the wired/primary network — treat it as its own isolated segment with no onward routing.
Change default admin credentials on every network-attached printer/MFP and disable unauthenticated raw-port printing where the fleet supports it.
Include printers and MFPs in the regular asset inventory and firmware-patching cycle rather than treating them as out-of-scope peripherals.

items.title: Insufficient Client Isolation
items.prerequisites: A device authorized to associate to the target SSID (guest or corporate). Standard network scanning tools (nmap, arp-scan). Written authorization to test lateral reachability between wireless clients.
items.whatItIs: Client isolation is a setting that stops devices on the same WiFi network from talking directly to each other — so a guest can reach the internet, but not another guest's laptop or an internal device's exposed services. Where it's turned off, misconfigured, or only applied to some access points and not others, devices sharing that WiFi network can reach each other directly.
items.rootCause: Client isolation has to be manually turned on and kept consistent across every access point — it's not something that's on by default. In environments with equipment from different vendors, or where settings drift over time, it's common for isolation to be correctly set on some access points and silently missing on others.
items.impact: On a guest network, one visitor's device can attack another directly, with no network barrier in between — exposed file shares, or an unpatched service. On a corporate segment the same gap allows lateral movement between employee devices. That turns a single compromised laptop into a foothold against every other device on the same network name.
stepsToIdentify: Associate two independent test devices to the same target SSID and attempt direct communication (ping, port scan) between them.
Repeat the test across every AP/controller in the deployment if the environment uses more than one, since isolation enforcement can vary by hardware/firmware version or configuration group.

Check for broadcast/multicast traffic visibility between clients (e.g. mDNS/Bonjour, NetBIOS) even where unicast isolation is correctly enforced, since some implementations isolate unicast but still forward multicast discovery traffic.

Review the wireless controller's isolation policy configuration directly where admin access is available, rather than relying solely on black-box testing, to confirm consistent application across SSIDs and AP groups.
Confirm isolation separately for unicast, broadcast and multicast, since controllers commonly block client-to-client unicast while leaving mDNS and SSDP discovery fully reachable.
Test isolation between clients on different APs as well as the same AP, because the setting is frequently enforced per-AP and fails across a controller-managed roam.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes lateral communication testing between wireless clients on the target SSID.
Associate two nominated test devices to the same SSID (repeating across different APs/controllers if the deployment has more than one).
Attempt ICMP and port-scan reachability from one test device to the other.

If reachable, attempt to access any exposed service on the second test device (a deliberately-configured test service, not a real production workload) to demonstrate practical lateral-movement impact.
Check for multicast/broadcast-based discovery leakage (mDNS, SSDP, NetBIOS) even if direct unicast reachability is blocked.
Document which APs/controllers correctly enforced isolation and which did not, since this is often an inconsistency finding rather than a uniform absence.

examplePayloads.label: Test direct reachability between two associated clients
Port scan a peer client on the same SSID
Check for multicast/broadcast discovery leakage
examplePayloads.command: tcpdump -i wlan0 'udp port 5353 or udp port 1900 or udp port 137'

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate other associated clients through ARP, which bypasses isolation that filters only IP forwarding
Confirm whether multicast discovery crosses the isolation boundary
Test reachability to a second nominated test client directly

variants: Isolation correctly enforced for unicast traffic but multicast/broadcast discovery protocols still forwarded between clients.
Isolation enforced inconsistently across a multi-AP/multi-controller deployment due to configuration drift between hardware generations or firmware versions.
Isolation enforced on the wireless controller but bypassed through the wired gateway, where traffic leaving and re-entering the segment is no longer subject to the client-to-client rule.
IPv6 link-local reachability retained while IPv4 isolation is correctly enforced, which is a frequent oversight because the control is written against the IPv4 path only.
mitigation: Enable and verify client isolation on every AP/controller serving guest and, where appropriate, corporate SSIDs — test after every configuration change or firmware upgrade rather than assuming it persists.
Explicitly filter multicast/broadcast discovery protocols (mDNS, SSDP, NetBIOS) between clients even where unicast isolation is enforced, if these aren't operationally required.
For corporate wireless, layer host-based firewalling and endpoint detection as a compensating control rather than relying on network isolation alone.
Standardize isolation policy centrally (via the wireless controller) rather than per-AP configuration to reduce drift risk in multi-AP deployments.

items.title: PMKID Attack (Clientless)
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode. hcxdumptool to request the PMKID from the target AP, and hashcat (GPU-accelerated) for offline cracking. Written authorization to capture and crack the PMKID, since this recovers a live production passphrase.
items.whatItIs: Many personal WiFi access points include a value called a PMKID — derived straight from the network password — in the very first message they send, originally added to help with fast roaming. An attacker can just ask the access point for this value directly, with a single message and no device or handshake required at all, then crack it offline exactly like they would a captured login handshake.
items.rootCause: The PMKID field was added purely as a roaming shortcut, but it's calculated from the same password-derived secret used in the main login process — and a lot of access points will hand it over to literally anyone who asks, even a device that never actually logs in. What was meant as a performance optimization became a way to steal password material without a real user or device ever being involved.
items.impact: The passphrase can be cracked offline without waiting for, or forcing, a client handshake. That removes the mitigation people traditionally rely on here: a network with no connected clients at all is still exposed. Once cracked, the consequences match the standard weak passphrase finding — full network access, and decryption of traffic captured earlier.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm the target AP responds to an unauthenticated PMKID request using hcxdumptool against a nominated test BSSID.
Check AP vendor/firmware for known PMKID-disclosure behavior, since not all implementations expose it and some have been patched to omit the field from the initial handshake message.

If a PMKID is obtained, attempt offline cracking against a curated wordlist within an agreed time/compute budget to establish real-world crackability, consistent with the process used for the weak-PSK finding.
Where a PMKID is not disclosed, note whether the AP firmware is a known-patched version, since this distinguishes 'not vulnerable' from 'not tested long enough to trigger it'.
Confirm whether the AP includes a PMKID in the first message of the handshake at all, since the attack depends on that field being populated and many current firmware versions omit it.
Establish whether the same PSK is in use across the estate, because a PMKID captured from one unattended AP then yields access everywhere that key is configured.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes clientless PMKID capture and offline cracking against the target BSSID.
Use hcxdumptool to send an association request to the target AP and capture the returned PMKID from the first EAPOL frame.
Convert the captured PMKID to hashcat format and run a GPU-accelerated attack using a wordlist tailored to the organization's likely conventions.
If successful, confirm the recovered passphrase by associating a test device, then stop — report the finding without further use of the recovered credential.

Where the AP does not respond with a PMKID, note this explicitly in the report as a positive finding (the AP is not vulnerable to this specific clientless technique), separate from whether the standard handshake-capture weak-PSK finding still applies.

examplePayloads.label: Request PMKID from the target AP (no client needed)
Convert captured PMKID for hashcat
GPU-accelerated PMKID crack
Capture PMKIDs from every AP in range without needing any client to be present
Convert the capture into a crackable hash
Run a targeted rule-based attack against the recovered PMKID

variants: Combined approach that falls back to standard handshake capture (with a bounded, authorized deauth) if the AP doesn't disclose a PMKID directly.

PMKID capture succeeds against the AP but the resulting hash proves uncrackable within a practical timeframe due to a genuinely high-entropy passphrase — still worth documenting as a confirmed-exposure/low-immediate-risk finding rather than a non-finding.
Collection while walking the perimeter, which gathers PMKIDs from every AP whose coverage leaves the building without any association or client interaction at all.
Targeting an out-of-hours or unattended site, where the absence of clients defeats handshake capture but has no effect on this technique.
mitigation: Apply vendor firmware updates that omit PMKID disclosure to unauthenticated stations where such patches are available.
Enforce the same long, high-entropy passphrase guidance as the weak-PSK finding, since a strong passphrase remains uncrackable regardless of whether the PMKID or a full handshake is obtained.
Migrate to WPA3-Personal (SAE) where all clients support it, since SAE's handshake design is not vulnerable to this offline PMKID-based dictionary attack.
Prefer WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with per-user credentials for any network where the risk of shared-passphrase compromise is unacceptable.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your wireless password can be attacked without anyone being connected and without any interaction. An attacker within range collects a single piece of data directly from the access point in seconds, then works on recovering the password elsewhere at their own pace. Because no client device is involved, an empty office at night is as good a target as a busy one — better, in fact, since there is nobody to notice. The defence is password strength, since the attack itself cannot be prevented: a long random passphrase makes recovery impractical. Moving corporate wireless to individual logins removes the shared password this attack targets altogether.

items.title: RF Jamming Denial of Service Susceptibility
items.prerequisites: An RF signal generator or a Wi-Fi adapter capable of continuous transmission/flooding within the target's operating band (2.4GHz/5GHz), used only in a shielded lab or otherwise fully authorized RF environment. Written authorization is mandatory and unusually strict here: intentional RF jamming is regulated by telecom authorities in most jurisdictions (e.g. FCC in the US, other national regulators elsewhere), so this test must be performed in a way that does not interfere with any device or network outside the engagement's explicit physical and spectrum scope.
items.whatItIs: Like any radio-based system, WiFi can simply be jammed — flooding the airwaves with enough noise that legitimate devices can't successfully communicate at all, no matter how strong the encryption or login process is. This is tested to check the organization's physical and operational readiness to detect and respond to jamming, not because jamming itself can be prevented through WiFi settings.
items.rootCause: Shared radio spectrum has no built-in access control at the physical level — anything transmitting strongly enough on the same channel blocks everyone else from using it, completely independent of encryption, login, or any other WiFi setting. This is a basic physical property of radio, not something a protocol fix can solve.
items.impact: Wireless service is denied completely for the duration and physical range of the jamming signal. It affects every device and every network on the affected channel simultaneously, regardless of protocol or encryption. For any operation that depends on wireless — point of sale, warehouse scanners, guest services — this is a business continuity risk, and there is no purely technical wireless-side mitigation available.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm with the client the exact legal/regulatory authorization and physical containment plan (shielded room, controlled test site) before any jamming activity is even considered, since unauthorized RF jamming is a regulatory offense in most countries independent of any penetration-testing engagement scope.

Where full active jamming is not authorized or feasible, assess susceptibility analytically instead: review whether the organization has any RF spectrum monitoring in place, whether critical operations have a wired/cellular fallback, and whether physical access to the RF environment (parking lots, adjacent floors) is controlled.

Check for existing spectrum analyzer or WIDS capability that would detect an actual jamming event in production, since detection/response readiness is usually the real deliverable for this finding rather than a live jamming demonstration.

Where full active jamming cannot be authorized, review the AP's channel-utilization and interference-history logs (if available) for evidence of prior, unexplained connectivity disruptions that may already indicate real-world susceptibility.

Establish which business processes stop when wireless stops — stock scanning, payment terminals, nurse call, voice handsets — since the finding's severity is set by that dependency rather than by the radio itself.
Confirm whether a wired or cellular fallback exists and has been tested, because an untested fallback is functionally absent during an outage.
exploitationSteps: Do not proceed with active RF jamming unless the engagement has explicit, documented legal authorization and physical containment (e.g. a shielded enclosure) — this differs from the deauthentication finding, which operates at the protocol layer within normal transmit power and does not carry the same regulatory exposure.

Where authorized and contained, generate a controlled interference signal on the target channel within the shielded environment only and confirm loss of legitimate association/throughput as proof of concept.

Measure and document the time-to-detect and time-to-alert if the client's WIDS/spectrum-monitoring tooling is in place, since this operational-response data is typically more valuable to the client than the jamming demonstration itself.

Where live jamming isn't authorized, deliver this finding as a documented susceptibility/resilience assessment (fallback connectivity, detection capability, incident-response plan) rather than a demonstrated exploit.

Recommend documented incident-response and fallback-connectivity procedures as the primary remediation where full RF hardening (shielding, spectrum monitoring) is not immediately feasible, since jamming resilience is rarely something a single technical control fully resolves.

examplePayloads.label: Continuous-transmission channel flood (shielded lab / fully authorized site ONLY)
examplePayloads.command: mdk4 wlan0mon m -t <target-bssid>  # RF-layer noise/flood test — never run outside an explicitly authorized, contained environment

examplePayloads.label: Spectrum analysis to confirm interference and measure channel occupancy
examplePayloads.command: iw dev wlan0 scan | grep -A2 signal  # or use a dedicated spectrum analyzer for accurate RF measurement

examplePayloads.label: Measure the noise floor and interference across the band to establish a baseline before testing
examplePayloads.command: sudo iw dev wlan0 survey dump

examplePayloads.label: Confirm the controller reports the interference rather than silently degrading (Cisco WLC)

variants: Reactive/selective jamming that targets only specific frame types (e.g. deauth-frame-triggered jamming) rather than continuous broadband noise, requiring more sophisticated equipment but harder to detect via simple spectrum monitoring.

Protocol-layer flooding (association-request or probe-request floods) as a lower-regulatory-risk proxy for full RF jamming, since it denies service via resource exhaustion rather than physical-layer noise.
Narrowband interference targeting only the control channel, which is far harder to attribute than broadband jamming while producing the same operational outcome.
Protocol-level denial through continuous CTS-to-self frames, which silences the cell using standards-compliant frames and needs no jamming hardware.
mitigation: Deploy spectrum analysis / WIDS capability that can detect and alert on abnormal RF interference or noise-floor changes on operating channels.
Maintain a documented fallback connectivity plan (wired, cellular failover) for business-critical operations that depend on wireless availability.
Where feasible, use multiple APs across non-overlapping channels/bands so a single-channel jamming event doesn't take down all wireless service simultaneously.

Establish an incident-response runbook specifically for suspected RF interference, including how to report it to the relevant telecom regulator if it appears to be a deliberate, unauthorized jamming attempt.
Maintain and periodically exercise a wired or cellular fallback for any process that stops when wireless stops, since the radio environment itself cannot be secured.
Enable and monitor the controller's spectrum intelligence so interference is raised as an alert rather than surfacing as unexplained user complaints.

The question this finding raises is therefore not how to stop it, but what in your business stops when wireless stops. Identify those processes, make sure each has a wired or mobile fallback, and test that fallback rather than assuming it works. Alongside that, enable interference alerting on your wireless controllers so that a deliberate disruption is recognised as one rather than being investigated for hours as an unexplained fault.

items.title: SSID Spoofing / Beacon Flooding
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and beacon-frame injection. mdk4 or a custom beacon-flooding script. Written authorization for active beacon spoofing/flooding within the target site.
items.whatItIs: An attacker broadcasts fake network announcements for names matching no real access point. One approach floods the area with hundreds of fake networks to confuse anyone trying to find the genuine one. The other copies the exact name of a trusted network — a lighter version of an Evil Twin that does not require anyone to actually connect.
items.rootCause: These network announcements aren't verified in any way — anyone can broadcast one claiming to be any network name, since WiFi has no mechanism to check whether the device sending the announcement is actually allowed to use that name.
items.impact: At minimum this creates user confusion and support load, as staff and visitors struggle to pick the real network out of the decoys. At worst it denies service to automated wireless security tooling, which can be overwhelmed by hundreds of fake networks. It also supplies a ready social engineering pretext, since a user who cannot tell which network is genuine will often ask someone, or simply guess.
stepsToIdentify: Monitor for beacon frames advertising SSIDs not present in the organization's documented AP inventory, particularly any using a naming pattern similar to legitimate networks.
Check whether wireless scanning/WIDS tooling in use has any documented behavior or resource limits when faced with a very high number of simultaneously-advertised SSIDs.

Assess whether staff/visitors have a reliable, documented way to identify the legitimate SSID (e.g. signage referencing an exact, unique name) versus relying on recognition alone, which beacon flooding specifically undermines.
Check whether client devices display any visual distinguishing indicator (network security icon, saved-network star) that would help a user avoid a convincingly-named decoy SSID during the flood.
Confirm whether the wireless controller raises an alert when an SSID it owns is advertised from an unknown BSSID, since without that the spoof is invisible to the operator.
Establish how client devices rank networks of the same name, because a client that selects purely on signal strength will prefer a nearby spoof over a distant genuine AP.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active beacon spoofing/flooding within the target site and agree a bounded duration to limit disruption to legitimate wireless scanning by staff/other tools.
Generate a bounded flood of forged beacon frames advertising a mix of decoy SSIDs, including at least one crafted to closely resemble the legitimate corporate SSID.
Observe and document the effect on standard wireless client scan lists (does the legitimate network become hard to distinguish or locate among the decoys).
If in scope, test whether the client's WIDS/security scanning tooling correctly continues to detect and alert despite the flood, or whether its detection degrades under load.
Stop the flood once the finding is proven; don't run it for longer than needed given its potential to disrupt other users' ability to connect to legitimate networks during the test window.

examplePayloads.label: Beacon flood with randomized decoy SSIDs
Spoof a beacon closely resembling the legitimate SSID
Identify every distinct BSSID advertising the corporate SSID and compare against inventory
Flood the environment with beacon frames to test detection and client behaviour under authorisation

variants: Targeted single-SSID spoofing designed to sit alongside the legitimate network as a decoy for social-engineering purposes, versus a broad, high-volume flood aimed at degrading scanning tools generally.

Beacon flooding combined with a simultaneous deauthentication campaign against the real AP, intended to make the flood of fake networks the path of least resistance for a confused or automated reconnecting client.
A single spoofed SSID matching the corporate name exactly, which is far stealthier than beacon flooding and is the shape used when the goal is association rather than disruption.
Beacon flooding used purely as cover, generating enough noise that a genuine rogue AP is lost among the alerts it produces.
mitigation: Deploy WIDS/WIPS capable of distinguishing forged/unauthorized beacons from the legitimate authorized inventory and alerting accordingly, with resource headroom to remain effective under a high-volume flood.

Provide staff/visitors with clear, specific guidance (exact SSID name, ideally paired with an out-of-band verification method) rather than relying on visual recognition among a potentially crowded list.
Where feasible, use 802.11w/PMF and enterprise authentication so that even if a user connects to a spoofed SSID, credential-based protections limit the impact.
Enable rogue-SSID alerting on the wireless controller so that the corporate SSID advertised from an unknown BSSID raises an alert rather than passing unnoticed.
Deploy 802.1X with server-certificate validation on managed clients, so that a device presented with a spoofed SSID cannot complete authentication regardless of signal strength.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Anyone nearby can broadcast networks using your organisation's name, or flood the area with hundreds of fake network names. The first is used to lure devices onto attacker equipment; the second causes confusion and hides the first. Your controllers can raise an alert when your own network name is broadcast from equipment you do not own, and that alerting is currently off — which means this could be happening now without your knowledge. Turn it on, and make sure the alerts reach someone who will act. Device-side certificate checking, recommended elsewhere in this report, is what stops a lure from succeeding even when one is running.

It is worth confirming and fixing early, before it is chained into something larger.

items.title: WPA/WPA2-PSK Weak Passphrase
items.prerequisites: Overlaps substantially with the weak-PSK-reuse finding (WIFI-012): a wireless adapter capable of monitor mode, hcxdumptool/hashcat or aircrack-ng, and written authorization to capture and crack the live passphrase. This item specifically covers passphrase strength/complexity as a standalone policy gap distinct from cross-network reuse.
items.whatItIs: This finding is specifically about the WiFi password itself being weak — short, a common word or phrase, or an easy-to-guess pattern like the company name or a keyboard pattern (separate from whether it's also reused elsewhere, which is tracked as its own finding). A weak password can be cracked with a simple dictionary attack against a captured login handshake, often in seconds to minutes on modern hardware.
items.rootCause: No minimum password strength was required when it was set, and it's never been reviewed since — so even though the underlying WPA2/WPA3 protocol is sound, the password itself is small enough to guess through straightforward offline cracking.
items.impact: Full network compromise follows quickly through offline dictionary cracking, often almost immediately. The limiting factor is password strength rather than any weakness in the protocol itself. A network with a weak passphrase should be treated as materially more likely to be compromised in the near term than one with a strong random passphrase, independent of how well the rest of the network is segmented.
stepsToIdentify: Capture the handshake or PMKID as described in the related PMKID/handshake-capture findings and run it against a standard dictionary (rockyou.txt and similar) plus a client-specific wordlist built from public company information.

Note the time-to-crack against a commodity GPU as the primary evidence of severity — a passphrase cracked in under an hour with a basic dictionary is materially worse than one that resists a multi-day attempt.

Review the organization's password/passphrase policy documentation, if any exists, specifically for wireless network secrets, since this is often an overlooked gap even in organizations with strong general password policy.

Cross-reference the recovered passphrase's structure (dictionary word, keyboard pattern, company-name-plus-year) against the organization's stated password policy to determine whether the wireless-specific policy is weaker than the general corporate one.

Build a site-specific candidate list from the organisation's public presence before using any general wordlist, since corporate passphrases are overwhelmingly derived from the company name, address or founding year.
Confirm how the passphrase would be changed if it were compromised, because a key embedded in hundreds of unmanaged devices cannot realistically be rotated and that constrains the remediation advice.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes handshake/PMKID capture and offline dictionary cracking of the live passphrase.
Capture the handshake (via a bounded, authorized deauth-and-recapture) or the PMKID directly if the AP discloses it.

Run a staged dictionary attack: common wordlists first, then a client-specific wordlist built from public OSINT (company name variations, address, product names), escalating only as far as the agreed time/compute budget allows.
Record the exact wordlist/rule stage at which the passphrase was recovered as evidence for the report's severity rationale.
Confirm the recovered passphrase with a single test association, then stop.

Staged dictionary attack: common wordlist first
Then a client-specific OSINT-built wordlist with mangling rules
Generate a targeted candidate list from organisation-specific terms
examplePayloads.command: hashcat --stdout -a 1 company_terms.txt years.txt | hashcat --stdout -r rules/best64.rule > targeted.txt

examplePayloads.label: Run the targeted list against the captured handshake before falling back to a general wordlist

variants: Weak passphrase following a predictable seasonal/incrementing pattern across rotations, compounding the weak-strength finding with a weak-rotation-policy finding.

A technically long passphrase that is nonetheless low-entropy (a common phrase, a keyboard-walk pattern, or the organization's name plus a predictable suffix) — passing a naive length-only policy check while remaining trivially crackable with a targeted wordlist.
A long passphrase that is nonetheless a predictable phrase, which resists brute force but falls immediately to a phrase-based wordlist.
The same passphrase reused as the wired network's management credential, where recovering it from the air yields administrative access rather than only network connectivity.
mitigation: Set a long (20+ character), randomly generated passphrase, distributed via a password manager rather than chosen for memorability.
Adopt a documented minimum-entropy standard for any shared wireless secret and periodically re-test crackability as part of routine wireless assessments.
Migrate to WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with per-user credentials wherever feasible, removing the shared-passphrase-strength problem entirely.
Where WPA3-Personal (SAE) is supported by all clients, prefer it, since SAE resists offline dictionary attacks even against comparatively weaker passphrases.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your wireless password was recovered during testing. It is based on recognisable details about the organisation, which is the first thing anyone attempting this tries — attackers build a candidate list from your own website before touching a general password list. The replacement should be long and random rather than memorable, since it is stored by devices and rarely typed. Before changing it, confirm how many devices hold the current one, because that count determines whether this is an afternoon's work or a project. If the answer is a large number of unmanaged devices, that itself is the stronger argument for moving to individual logins.

items.title: WPA3 Dragonblood Vulnerabilities
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and packet injection, and precise timing-measurement capability (or a cache-timing-capable co-located process for the cache-based variant) for the SAE handshake. The Dragonblood research team's published proof-of-concept tooling. Written authorization to actively probe the target's SAE handshake implementation, since timing measurements typically require repeated live handshake attempts.
items.whatItIs: Dragonblood is a set of vulnerabilities found in WPA3's newer login process (SAE), which was specifically designed to resist the offline password-guessing attacks that plague WPA2. The main issue: some implementations leaked subtle timing or memory-access clues during password processing, which was enough for an attacker to still mount an efficient offline guessing attack — defeating the whole point of the upgrade. A separate issue lets an attacker force a device that supports both WPA2 and WPA3 to fall back to the weaker WPA2 login instead.
items.rootCause: SAE, the new login method, is soundly designed in theory — but several real implementations processed the password using code whose timing or memory access pattern varied depending on the secret password itself, and that kind of leak is exactly what side-channel attacks are built to catch. The separate downgrade issue exists because WPA3-Transition mode intentionally supports both old and new devices on the same network for compatibility — and an attacker can abuse that flexibility to force the weaker option.
items.impact: Where the side-channel is present and exploitable, an attacker recovers enough from a modest number of observed handshakes to run an accelerated offline dictionary attack against the passphrase. That reintroduces exactly the weak-passphrase cracking risk WPA3 was designed to eliminate. The downgrade variant is separate but equally serious: it forces a client in transition mode back onto WPA2, exposing it to every WPA2 weakness documented elsewhere.
stepsToIdentify: Identify AP vendor/firmware and cross-reference against the Dragonblood advisory list and subsequent vendor patch notes for that specific model.
Confirm whether the network operates in WPA3-only or WPA3-Transition (mixed WPA2/WPA3) mode, since the downgrade variant only applies to transition mode.
With authorization, attempt the published Dragondrain/Dragontime/Dragonslayer proof-of-concept tests against the target AP to check for timing variance correlated with password guesses.
For transition-mode networks, attempt to force a WPA3-capable test client to negotiate WPA2 instead and confirm whether the downgrade succeeds.
Confirm the AP firmware version against the vendor's Dragonblood advisory, since this is a patching finding and the presence of WPA3 alone does not indicate exposure.
Check whether WPA3 is deployed in transition mode, because the downgrade path there is a larger exposure than the side-channel weaknesses themselves.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active SAE-handshake side-channel testing and, separately, downgrade-attack testing against a nominated test client.

Run the published Dragonblood proof-of-concept tooling against the target AP, submitting repeated handshake attempts with varying candidate passwords and measuring response timing/behavior for statistically significant variance.
If a usable side channel is found, use the leaked information to prioritize an offline dictionary attack and demonstrate accelerated cracking versus a naive attack with no side-channel data.

Separately, on a WPA3-Transition-mode SSID, attempt to force a nominated dual-mode test client to complete a WPA2 handshake instead of SAE, then treat the resulting connection as subject to standard WPA2-class findings (weak-PSK, KRACK) for further testing if in scope.
Report findings against the specific AP firmware version tested, since Dragonblood remediation is almost entirely a vendor-patch matter.

Test WPA3-Transition downgrade to WPA2 for a dual-mode client

examplePayloads.label: Confirm whether the AP also advertises WPA2, which indicates transition mode and an available downgrade
examplePayloads.command: sudo airodump-ng --essid '<target-ssid>' wlan0mon  # the ENC column shows WPA2 WPA3 when both are offered

variants: Cache-based side-channel variant (exploiting shared-hardware cache timing) as opposed to the network-observable timing variant, relevant primarily where an attacker has co-located code execution rather than pure over-the-air access.
Group-negotiation downgrade forcing a weaker elliptic-curve group during SAE rather than a full WPA2 downgrade.
Downgrade to WPA2 against an AP in transition mode, which sidesteps SAE entirely and is materially easier than exploiting the side channels.
Resource-exhaustion denial of service against the SAE commit exchange, which is cheap to mount and affects patched and unpatched firmware alike.
mitigation: Apply vendor firmware/software patches addressing the specific Dragonblood CVEs (CVE-2019-9494 through CVE-2019-9498) for both APs and any client devices with WPA3 supplicant support.
Where feasible and all clients support it, run WPA3-only rather than WPA3-Transition mode, eliminating the downgrade-to-WPA2 vector entirely.
Track WPA3/SAE-specific advisories from the Wi-Fi Alliance and chipset vendors as a distinct patch-management stream, since these are newer and less mature than WPA2-era guidance.
Re-test SAE handshake timing behavior after any firmware upgrade claiming to remediate Dragonblood, since some vendor patches have historically been incomplete.
items.mitigationClientFacing: You are running WPA3, which is the right choice and a meaningful improvement over what came before. This finding is narrower: the firmware here predates the vendor fixes for a known set of weaknesses in it, so the benefit is not fully realised. Updating the firmware resolves it. Worth flagging separately is that the network is running in a mode that also accepts the older WPA2 standard so that legacy devices still work. That fallback is a larger exposure than the firmware issue, because an attacker can simply take the older path. Plan to retire it once the remaining older devices are replaced.

items.title: WPS PIN Vulnerability
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and packet injection. Reaver or Bully for online PIN brute-forcing, or the Pixie Dust offline variant tooling where the target AP's chipset is vulnerable. Written authorization for active WPS PIN attack against the target AP.
items.whatItIs: WPS PIN mode was meant to make setup easier — an 8-digit PIN instead of a full password. But the PIN gets checked in two separate halves, which means an attacker learns whether the first half is right before even guessing the second — shrinking the realistic number of guesses needed from 100 million down to around 11,000. That's crackable online in a few hours, or in minutes via 'Pixie Dust,' an offline attack that works against routers with weak random-number generation.
items.rootCause: The WPS design checks an 8-digit PIN as two separate pieces instead of all at once, so an attacker gets confirmation on the first half before guessing the second — and the very last digit isn't even a real guess, it's just a checksum. Together, this shrinks the realistic keyspace by orders of magnitude. Separately, several router makers generated the random values used during WPS setup so predictably that the entire PIN can be recovered offline from a single handshake, no guessing required.
items.impact: Recovering the WPS PIN yields the full passphrase directly, because WPS is designed to hand the passphrase over once the PIN validates. The attacker then has complete network access. The strength of the underlying passphrase is irrelevant here: a randomly generated 20-character passphrase provides no protection at all while vulnerable WPS PIN mode remains enabled.
stepsToIdentify: Confirm WPS is enabled on the target AP and check the WPS information element for the specific state (PIN method enabled/disabled/locked).
Identify AP chipset/vendor from the OUI and beacon fingerprint and check against the published list of Pixie-Dust-vulnerable chipsets.
With authorization, run Reaver/Bully in a bounded test to confirm whether online PIN brute-forcing is rate-limited/locked out by the AP after repeated failures, or proceeds unrestricted.
Where the chipset is a known Pixie Dust candidate, attempt a single WPS handshake capture and offline PIN recovery to confirm exploitability without needing extended online brute-forcing.
Confirm whether WPS is advertised in the beacon and whether the external registrar PIN method is enabled, since the push-button method alone is not exposed to this attack.
Establish whether WPS was re-enabled by a firmware update or factory reset, which is a common cause of it reappearing on a network where it was previously disabled.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorizes active WPS PIN attacks (online brute-force and/or offline Pixie Dust) against the target AP.
If the AP's chipset is a known Pixie-Dust candidate, capture a single WPS registration handshake and run the offline attack to attempt PIN/passphrase recovery within minutes.

If Pixie Dust isn't applicable, run a bounded online PIN brute-force (Reaver/Bully) and monitor for AP lockout behavior; document whether the AP correctly rate-limits or locks after repeated failed attempts.
Once the PIN is recovered, confirm the resulting WPA2/WPA3 passphrase and verify network association, then stop.

Report the specific attack class that succeeded (online split-PIN brute-force vs. offline Pixie Dust) since remediation guidance differs — a chipset-level nonce fix requires a firmware update, whereas the split-PIN keyspace issue requires disabling WPS PIN mode entirely.

variants: Pixie Dust offline attack exploiting weak nonce generation (near-instant recovery on vulnerable chipsets) versus the classic online split-PIN brute-force (hours, and rate-limitable by the AP).
Push-button configuration (PBC) mode abuse, a related but distinct WPS method that can be raced or replayed under certain AP implementations.
The Pixie Dust offline attack, which recovers the PIN in seconds from a single exchange where the AP generates weak nonces, rather than requiring an online guessing run.
WPS silently re-enabled after a firmware upgrade or factory reset, which is the usual reason the finding recurs on a network where it was previously remediated.
mitigation: Disable WPS entirely — this is the only complete fix; WPS's PIN-splitting design flaw cannot be configured around while the feature remains enabled.
Where WPS cannot be disabled (some consumer-grade hardware enables it un-disable-ably in certain firmware versions), replace the AP hardware.
Apply vendor firmware updates addressing Pixie-Dust-class nonce-generation weaknesses if WPS must remain temporarily enabled for operational reasons.
Audit the wireless estate specifically for WPS status as a standalone check, since it's frequently overlooked even when passphrase strength and encryption type are otherwise well-managed.
items.mitigationClientFacing: A convenience feature that lets devices join wireless by pressing a button or entering a short number is enabled here. The number can be worked out by an attacker within range, in some cases within seconds, and it yields the full wireless password. Turn the feature off. Two things are worth knowing: it is often re-enabled silently by a firmware update or a factory reset, so it needs re-checking after maintenance rather than being fixed once, and a device that already uses it will need to be rejoined manually, which is worth scheduling rather than discovering.

items.title: 802.1X / RADIUS EAP Method Downgrade & MAB Bypass
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and packet injection, hostapd-mana or eaphammer for rogue EAP server simulation, physical or RF proximity to the target WLAN, and knowledge of the deployed EAP method(s) (PEAP-MSCHAPv2, EAP-TLS, EAP-FAST).
items.whatItIs: Enterprise Wi-Fi networks using per-user logins can be attacked two ways. The first tricks a device into using a weaker, easier-to-crack login method than intended. The second targets networks that fall back to checking only a device's MAC address for equipment that cannot perform a full login: faking an authorised device's address gets the attacker onto the network with no credentials at all.
items.rootCause: Devices are often set up to accept several different login methods without being locked to the strongest one, and without properly checking the login server's certificate — which lets a rogue access point offer a weaker method and capture crackable login data. Separately, MAC-based fallback access trusts a device's address as proof of identity, even though addresses are trivial to fake.
items.impact: Downgrade attacks yield challenge and response pairs that can often be cracked offline, or exchanged for a reusable hash, to obtain valid domain credentials. Those credentials typically work well beyond the wireless network. Separately, MAC-based fallback lets unauthorised devices onto the same trusted network segment as legitimate, properly authenticated endpoints.
stepsToIdentify: Passively survey the target WLAN's beacon/probe traffic to identify supported EAP methods advertised by the legitimate infrastructure.

Stand up a rogue AP using hostapd-mana configured to offer a weaker EAP method (e.g. PEAP-MSCHAPv2) with the same SSID and observe whether nearby client devices attempt to authenticate against it, indicating the client does not enforce server certificate/method pinning.
Capture the MSCHAPv2 challenge/response exchange from any client that connects to the rogue AP.

Separately, identify network ports or wireless segments using MAB by observing whether a device with no 802.1X supplicant is granted access purely based on a fixed MAC address, and test cloning an observed authorized MAC address onto an attacker device to see if it is likewise granted access.
Document whether client devices validate the RADIUS server's certificate chain (a properly configured supplicant should reject the rogue AP's self-signed or mismatched certificate).
exploitationSteps: Deploy the rogue AP/RADIUS combination (hostapd-mana or eaphammer) mimicking the target SSID and offering the weaker EAP method.
Wait for or lure a client device to associate and attempt authentication, capturing the MSCHAPv2 handshake.
Crack the captured MSCHAPv2 response offline using asleap with a wordlist, or submit the DES-encrypted response to a cloud MSCHAPv2 cracking service to recover the underlying NTLM hash.
For the MAB path, clone the target's authorized MAC address onto an attacker-controlled NIC and confirm the attacker device is granted the same network access without any credential exchange.

Recommend enforcing certificate validation and a single, explicitly-approved EAP method on all managed supplicants via mobile device management (MDM) policy, since this closes the downgrade path at the client rather than relying solely on infrastructure hardening.

Test whether an unauthenticated device is admitted by MAC authentication bypass

variants: EAP-FAST PAC file interception and reuse when provisioning is done insecurely (anonymous PAC provisioning).
RADIUS shared-secret brute forcing where a weak, guessable shared secret between the AP and RADIUS server allows an attacker with wired access to impersonate the RADIUS server directly.
MAB bypass combined with VLAN hopping once initial network access is obtained, extending impact beyond the isolated MAB segment.
mitigation: Enforce EAP-TLS with mutual certificate authentication as the sole permitted EAP method where feasible, disabling weaker methods like PEAP-MSCHAPv2 and EAP-FAST entirely.
Configure client supplicants to strictly validate the RADIUS server's certificate (including CA pinning) and refuse to connect to networks presenting an unrecognized or self-signed certificate.

Avoid MAB wherever possible; where required for legacy devices, isolate MAB-authenticated devices into a tightly restricted VLAN with no access to sensitive resources and monitor for MAC address anomalies (e.g. the same MAC appearing on multiple ports/locations simultaneously).
Use long, high-entropy RADIUS shared secrets and rotate them periodically.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your corporate wireless uses individual logins, which is the right design. Two gaps were found in how it is enforced. Weaker login methods remain available and an attacker can request one instead of the strong method, and there is an approved-device list that admits equipment by an identifier which can simply be copied. Disable the weaker methods on the authentication server so the strong one is the only option, and treat the device list as an inventory convenience rather than a security control — anything relying on it for access should be moved behind proper authentication.

items.title: Absent or Ineffective Rogue Access Point Detection (WIDS/WIPS Coverage Gap)
items.prerequisites: Written authorisation to transmit on the target site's RF environment, including agreement that a test access point may briefly broadcast an SSID resembling the corporate one. A wireless adapter capable of access-point mode. A named client contact in the security operations team who can confirm whether an alert was generated, since the entire finding depends on the defender's side rather than the attacker's. Physical presence at the site, or a cooperating on-site participant.
items.whatItIs: Every offensive wireless technique in this domain assumes the attacker's transmitter goes unnoticed, and that assumption is almost never verified. This case tests it directly: stand up a controlled test access point and measure whether the organisation detects it, how long detection takes, whether anyone is alerted, and whether anyone acts. It is a detection and response finding rather than a vulnerability — the question is not whether a rogue AP can be created, which it always can, but whether the organisation would ever know.
items.rootCause: Wireless intrusion detection is frequently either absent, deployed only at headquarters while branch sites are unmonitored, or present but generating alerts nobody reviews. Where a controller offers rogue detection as a feature it is often left at a default that classifies neighbouring networks as rogue too, producing enough noise that genuine detections are lost among them. The underlying reason is that wireless monitoring sits between the network and physical security teams and is frequently owned by neither.
items.impact: Without detection, an evil twin, a Karma responder, or an unauthorised AP plugged into the corporate LAN can operate indefinitely. That converts every other wireless finding from a time-boxed opportunity into persistent access, and it removes the compensating control organisations typically cite when accepting the risk of a wireless weakness. It also means an employee-installed AP bypassing perimeter controls could sit on the network for months, which is the most common real-world occurrence of this issue and rarely malicious in intent.
stepsToIdentify: Establish whether a wireless intrusion detection or prevention capability exists at all, and whether it covers this specific site rather than only the primary office.
Determine how rogue classification is configured — whether it distinguishes an AP plugged into the corporate LAN from a neighbouring business's legitimate network.

Ask the security operations team what a rogue AP alert looks like on their side, and whether any have been raised in the past year, since a long silence usually indicates absent coverage rather than a clean environment.
Conduct a passive survey to inventory every AP visible at the site, and compare it against the organisation's own asset list — a mismatch is a finding before any transmission occurs.
Check whether wired-side controls (802.1X on access ports, port security) would independently prevent an unauthorised AP from being plugged in.
Confirm who is expected to respond to a detection and within what timeframe, since a detection nobody owns is functionally the same as no detection.
exploitationSteps: Agree the test SSID, its duration, the exact time window, and the halt procedure in writing before transmitting anything, and confirm no client devices are expected to join.
Start with the least intrusive variant: broadcast a distinctly-named test SSID that no employee device would ever auto-join, and measure whether it is detected.
Record the elapsed time between first transmission and any alert reaching a human, distinguishing detection by a system from detection by a person.
If the benign SSID goes unnoticed, escalate as agreed to an SSID resembling the corporate one, since detection frequently keys on name similarity — but keep the window short and monitored.
Do not allow real client devices to associate; use a fixed test client if association behaviour must be demonstrated at all.
Shut down the test AP at the agreed time regardless of outcome, confirm with the client that no residual alerts remain open, and report the detection time as the primary metric.
