variants: Detection present but unowned, where the system raises an alert that reaches a queue nobody monitors — technically detected, operationally invisible.
Coverage gaps at branch or satellite sites while headquarters is monitored, which is the most common real-world pattern.
Alert fatigue where neighbouring businesses are classified as rogue, burying genuine detections in noise.
Detection without containment, where the system identifies a rogue AP but has no automated or procedural response to remove it.
mitigation: Deploy wireless intrusion detection covering every site where corporate wireless operates, not only the primary office.
Tune rogue classification to distinguish an AP bridged onto the corporate LAN from a neighbouring network, so alerts stay actionable.
Assign explicit ownership and a target response time for rogue AP alerts, since an unowned alert is equivalent to no detection.
Enforce 802.1X on wired access ports so an unauthorised AP cannot obtain network access even if it goes undetected over the air.
Maintain an accurate inventory of authorised access points, since rogue detection is only meaningful relative to a known-good baseline.
Rehearse the response: periodically stand up an authorised test AP and measure detection-to-response time as an operational metric rather than assuming the capability works.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Every other wireless finding in this report assumes an attacker's equipment goes unnoticed, and we tested that assumption directly by operating a test access point on site. It was not detected, and no alert was raised. That matters because it changes the character of every other item here: without detection, a temporary opportunity becomes permanent access. It also means an access point plugged in by an employee for convenience — by far the most common real occurrence — could sit on your network indefinitely. Enable rogue detection on your controllers, tune it so neighbouring businesses do not drown out real alerts, and agree who responds.

items.title: WPA3 Transition Mode Downgrade to WPA2
items.prerequisites: A wireless network advertised as WPA3 but operating in transition mode, where WPA2 clients are still accepted on the same SSID. A wireless adapter supporting monitor mode and packet injection. Written authorisation covering rogue access point deployment and offline handshake cracking, since the attack captures material from real clients.
items.whatItIs: Transition mode exists so older clients keep working while an estate migrates, and it does that by accepting both WPA3-SAE and WPA2-PSK on one SSID. The security of the network therefore falls to WPA2 for any client that can be persuaded to use it. An attacker stands up a rogue access point advertising the same SSID with only WPA2 offered; a capable client associates using the weaker method and the resulting handshake is crackable offline. The organisation believes it deployed WPA3.
items.rootCause: Transition mode is a compatibility compromise, and the protection SAE provides against offline dictionary attack only holds if SAE is actually used. Because both methods share one passphrase, breaking the WPA2 handshake yields the credential for the WPA3 network too. Most clients do not warn when they associate with the weaker method, and most deployments are left in transition mode indefinitely because nothing visibly breaks.
items.impact: The offline dictionary resistance that motivated the WPA3 upgrade is lost entirely, and a weak passphrase becomes crackable exactly as it was before. items.title: OWE Transition Mode and Open Guest Network Downgrade
items.prerequisites: A guest or public network using Opportunistic Wireless Encryption, typically in transition mode where an open SSID is advertised alongside the encrypted one. A wireless adapter with monitor mode. Authorisation covering rogue access point deployment on a guest network, and agreement on whether guest traffic may be captured, since it may include non-employee users.
items.whatItIs: OWE gives an open network encryption without a passphrase, which is a real improvement over a plain open network. Transition mode preserves compatibility by advertising a hidden open SSID alongside it, and clients that do not support OWE join the open one. An attacker advertising only the open variant collects clients whose traffic is then unencrypted. Users see the same network name they always join and have no indication which variant they landed on.
items.rootCause: The transition design deliberately accepts an unencrypted fallback so that older clients keep working. Nothing in the client interface distinguishes an OWE association from an open one, so the user cannot tell and will not be warned. OWE also provides no authentication of the access point, meaning even a correct OWE association gives no assurance that the network is the intended one — it protects against passive interception, not against an adversary in the middle.
items.impact: Guest traffic that the organisation believes is encrypted is transmitted in the clear for any client the attacker captures. Anything not protected by transport encryption above the link layer is readable, including plaintext protocols and metadata such as hostnames. Because guest networks commonly carry personal devices, the exposure often extends to non-employees, which changes the reporting obligations. The finding is also frequently missed because the controller reports OWE as enabled.
stepsToIdentify: Capture beacons and identify whether both an OWE SSID and an open transition SSID are present.
Inspect the OWE transition element in the beacon to confirm the pairing between the two SSIDs.
Associate a client that lacks OWE support and confirm it lands on the open variant with no user-visible warning.
Check whether the guest network enforces any form of captive portal authentication after association.
Determine whether client isolation is enabled on the guest network, since that limits what a captured client is exposed to.
Establish what the organisation believes is deployed, since the gap between belief and configuration is often the finding.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope, and agree explicitly whether guest client traffic may be captured given that it may involve non-employees.
Record the target beacon configuration including the SSID pair and channel.
Advertise an open access point using the guest SSID, with no OWE element.
Observe which clients associate, and confirm from captured frames that the association is unencrypted.
Demonstrate visibility with metadata only — hostnames and plaintext requests — rather than capturing content, unless content capture is separately authorised.
Record how many clients preferred the rogue open network, as that number is what quantifies the exposure.

items.title: Guest-to-Corporate Wireless Segmentation Failure
items.prerequisites: A guest wireless network alongside corporate wireless on the same infrastructure. Credentials or open access to the guest network, which is typically available from reception or a printed notice. Authorisation to scan from the guest segment toward internal ranges, with agreed target ranges and a defined stop point before any exploitation of a reachable service.
items.whatItIs: Guest wireless is usually treated as a convenience rather than as a network boundary, and the configuration is often done once at installation and never reviewed. The question this case answers is narrow and practical: from a device on the guest network, what internal systems can actually be reached? Common findings are reachable management interfaces, a DNS or DHCP server answering from the corporate range, printers, and building systems that were placed on the wrong VLAN.
items.rootCause: Segmentation is implemented on the wireless controller as a VLAN assignment and assumed to be enforced end to end, while the actual enforcement depends on firewall rules at the boundary that are frequently permissive or absent. Shared services such as DNS, NTP and print are deliberately exposed to guests for convenience, and each exposure is a path. Changes made for a specific need, such as a temporary contractor requirement, are rarely reverted.
items.impact: An attacker needs only to be within wireless range and obtain a guest password that is often printed on a wall. From there, reachable internal services provide a foothold that bypasses every perimeter control the organisation operates. A reachable management interface on network hardware is the most serious common outcome, since default or weak credentials there yield control of the infrastructure that implements the segmentation in the first place.
stepsToIdentify: Obtain guest access through the normal route and record how easily it was obtained and whether it expires.
Determine the address assigned to a guest client, the gateway, and the DNS servers offered.
Establish whether the offered DNS resolver sits in the corporate range, which is a common and revealing misconfiguration.
Scan the guest segment first to determine whether client isolation is enforced between guests.
Probe agreed internal ranges to map what is reachable, distinguishing filtered from closed from open.
Identify the function of anything reachable, prioritising management interfaces, directory services and file shares.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope names the internal ranges that may be probed and the point at which testing stops.
Connect as an ordinary guest and capture the full DHCP offer including all options.
Test reachability of the gateway's own management interface, which is frequently exposed to the segment it serves.
Sweep the agreed internal ranges for responsive hosts and identify the services found.
For any management interface reached, confirm accessibility and stop at the login prompt rather than attempting credentials unless authorised.
Document each reachable service with the evidence that it was reached from the guest segment specifically.

Rotate guest credentials on a schedule and prefer per-visitor vouchers over a shared printed password.

From the guest network it was possible to reach systems that should only be reachable internally. Tighten the separation at the firewall so that guest traffic can reach the internet and nothing else, then re-test rather than assuming the rule change worked, since these paths are frequently reopened by a later, unrelated change.

items.title: Unauthorised Tethering and Ad-Hoc Bridging from Corporate Endpoints
items.prerequisites: Corporate endpoints with wireless adapters capable of acting as an access point, which covers essentially all current laptops. A wireless adapter with monitor mode for discovery. Authorisation to survey and to associate with any unauthorised access point found, and agreement on whether the endpoint behind it may be examined.
items.whatItIs: An employee who turns on a mobile hotspot, or connects to a phone's tethered network while docked, creates a path from outside the network straight onto a machine that is inside it. The bridge is built by a trusted user for an ordinary reason such as poor coverage or a blocked site. Nothing malicious happens, and the organisation's perimeter now has an undocumented opening for as long as the adapter stays on.
items.rootCause: Operating systems let a standard user enable hotspot and ad-hoc modes without administrative rights, because the feature is aimed at consumers. Endpoint configuration baselines frequently omit the setting because it is not obviously security-relevant. Wireless intrusion detection, where deployed, is usually tuned to find rogue access points advertising corporate SSIDs and will not flag a laptop broadcasting a personal network name.
items.impact: A bridged endpoint gives an attacker within wireless range a route onto a domain-joined machine while bypassing the perimeter firewall, proxy and inspection entirely. If the endpoint is simultaneously on the wired network, the bridge may extend further inward depending on routing and forwarding configuration. Tethered connections also remove the organisation's visibility of that machine's traffic completely, so any compromise that occurs over the tether is invisible to network monitoring.

Correlate the MAC address prefixes of unknown access points against vendor ranges typical of laptops and phones.
Check endpoint configuration policy for any restriction on hotspot, ad-hoc and Wi-Fi Direct modes.
Look for endpoints with two active network interfaces simultaneously, which indicates a potential bridge.
Review whether wireless intrusion detection alerts on any unauthorised access point or only on SSID impersonation.
Assess whether endpoint telemetry would show traffic that bypassed the corporate network path.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers surveying and associating with unauthorised access points discovered on site.
Conduct a walkthrough survey during working hours, since these networks appear and disappear with user activity.
Record each unauthorised access point with its SSID, BSSID, encryption and approximate location.
Associate where permitted and determine whether the host offers any service or routes toward internal addresses.
Establish whether the host is simultaneously connected to the corporate network, since that is what makes it a bridge.
Stop at demonstrating the bridge and report per device, since remediation is per endpoint and per policy.

items.title: Wi-Fi Easy Connect (DPP) Onboarding Weaknesses
items.prerequisites: A network using Device Provisioning Protocol onboarding, commonly deployed for headless IoT devices and increasingly for guest and staff onboarding by QR code. Physical or photographic access to a provisioning code, or the ability to place one. A wireless adapter with monitor mode for observing the exchange, and authorisation covering onboarding an unauthorised device.
items.whatItIs: DPP replaces a shared passphrase with a public key exchanged out of band, usually as a QR code, and the cryptography is sound. The weakness is almost always in how the code is handled. A code printed on a label, displayed on a screen, or left in a shared document is a credential, and it is rarely treated as one. Anyone who photographs it can often enrol a device, because the bootstrapping key is the whole of the authorisation.
items.rootCause: Deployment guidance focuses on the protocol rather than on the lifecycle of the code, so codes are commonly printed on device labels, posted in shared areas, or left in onboarding documentation. Many implementations accept the same code repeatedly instead of invalidating it after first use. Where a configurator role is delegated broadly, the number of people able to authorise a new device onto the network is larger than anyone intends.
items.impact: A photographed or reused code lets an unauthorised device join the network with legitimate credentials, appearing in logs as a properly onboarded device rather than an intrusion. On an IoT segment that may be limited, but DPP is increasingly used for general access, where the consequence is a foothold on the corporate network. Because the enrolment is cryptographically valid, detection depends entirely on device inventory discipline rather than on any protocol-level signal.
stepsToIdentify: Establish where DPP is in use and for which device classes, since IoT and general access carry very different consequences.
Determine how bootstrapping codes are distributed: printed labels, screens, email, or a documentation system.
Check whether a code is invalidated after first successful use or remains valid indefinitely.
Identify who holds the configurator role and whether that is a small named set or a broad group.
Assess whether codes are ever rotated, particularly after a device is decommissioned or returned.
Review whether newly onboarded devices are reconciled against an approved inventory, and how quickly.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope permits onboarding a tester device and agree how it will be removed afterwards.
Locate a bootstrapping code through the normal environment: device labels, shared documentation, or a displayed screen.
Record how the code was obtained and whether any access control stood between the tester and it.
Attempt enrolment of a tester device using that code and observe whether it succeeds.
Attempt a second enrolment with the same code to establish whether single use is enforced.
Confirm what network access the enrolled device received, and whether its appearance triggered any alert.

items.title: IoT and OT Device SoftAP Provisioning Exposure
items.prerequisites: Wireless IoT or operational technology devices that expose their own access point for setup: cameras, sensors, controllers, building systems and similar. A wireless adapter for discovery and association. Authorisation to associate with device-hosted access points and interact with their provisioning interfaces, with a clear stop point before changing any device configuration.
items.whatItIs: Most wireless IoT devices ship with a setup mode that broadcasts their own access point so a phone can configure them. The intent is that this mode closes once setup completes. In practice devices are frequently found still broadcasting it months later, either because provisioning never completed cleanly, or because the device re-enters setup mode after a power cycle, or because the firmware simply never disables it. That access point is usually open and its configuration interface usually unauthenticated.
items.rootCause: Setup mode is designed for convenience during a one-time operation and the security posture reflects that: open network, no authentication, full configuration access. Manufacturers assume the window is brief and physically supervised. Devices are commonly installed by facilities contractors rather than IT, so nobody verifies afterwards that setup mode closed. Power cycles during maintenance frequently reopen it with no notification to anyone.
items.impact: An open provisioning access point typically allows reading the stored wireless credentials the device uses for the production network, which yields the passphrase directly. It also permits reconfiguring the device to associate with an attacker-controlled network, and on operational technology it may expose control functions with safety consequences. Because these devices are rarely in the asset inventory, neither the exposure nor a subsequent compromise is likely to be noticed.
stepsToIdentify: Survey for access points whose SSIDs match manufacturer setup patterns, typically a vendor name with a serial or MAC fragment.
Identify the manufacturer from the BSSID prefix and the SSID naming convention.
Determine whether each provisioning access point is open or protected, and whether it is persistent across a power cycle.
Associate where permitted and identify the provisioning interface, usually a web service on the default gateway address.
Check whether the interface requires authentication, and whether any default credential is documented publicly.
Establish whether the stored production wireless credentials are readable through the interface.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope covers association and read-only interaction, and agree explicitly that no device configuration will be changed.
Survey during a walkthrough and record every device-hosted access point with its location.
Associate with one and enumerate the provisioning service on the assigned gateway address.
Access the configuration interface and record whether authentication was required at any point.
Where stored wireless credentials are exposed, capture the minimum evidence proving exposure without recording the passphrase in the report body.
Stop before modifying configuration, and report per device class since remediation is usually a firmware or process change across a fleet.

items.title: Staff Auto-Connecting to Open / Evil-Twin Networks
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of AP mode within radio range of staff or their devices, and a rogue-AP toolkit (hostapd-mana, EAPHammer, or Wifiphisher). No cracking is required — this test measures whether people and their preconfigured devices will join an untrusted open network. Written authorization must explicitly cover broadcasting a look-alike open SSID and observing real staff/device behaviour, because success depends on genuine users associating.
items.whatItIs: Many phones and laptops are configured to automatically rejoin any network whose name matches one they have saved — including open networks like 'attwifi', 'Starbucks', or a company's own open guest SSID. An attacker in a car park or lobby can broadcast that exact name, and staff devices will silently connect with no prompt at all. This test measures how many people, and how many corporate devices, will hand their traffic to an unknown access point purely because the network name looks familiar. It is fundamentally an awareness and configuration-hygiene finding, not a cryptographic one.
items.rootCause: Open networks offer no way for a device to verify it is joining the real access point, and most operating systems default to auto-joining saved open SSIDs by name alone. Staff are rarely trained that a familiar network name proves nothing, so both the human and the device treat the name as trust. The organisation has neither removed risky saved networks from managed devices nor taught users to distrust them.
items.impact: Every device that auto-joins the rogue AP exposes its traffic to interception, DNS hijacking, and captive-portal credential phishing. Because the join is silent, the user has no moment of decision at which to hesitate, so awareness of network hygiene is the only remaining defence. A single associated corporate laptop can leak session tokens, internal hostnames, and cached credentials before the user notices anything. Repeated across a workforce, this turns a public-space presence into a reliable interception channel.
items.realWorldContext: This is the everyday reality behind 'evil twin' warnings on airport and coffee-shop networks: the DEF CON 'Wall of Sheep' has for years demonstrated how many attendees' devices silently rejoin open SSIDs and leak credentials without their owners doing anything. In corporate engagements it is common to park outside an office, broadcast a common open SSID, and watch dozens of staff phones associate within minutes. The business consequence is that awareness training and saved-network hygiene, not encryption, decide the outcome — a workforce trained to distrust familiar names is far harder to harvest from.
stepsToIdentify: Run a passive capture with airodump-ng and extract client probe requests to build a list of open SSID names that staff devices are actively searching for (attwifi, xfinitywifi, common airport/hotel names, the company's own open guest SSID).
Review whether managed corporate devices carry saved open networks in their Wi-Fi profiles, and whether any MDM/GPO policy removes or blocks auto-join for non-corporate SSIDs.
Interview the wireless and security-awareness teams on whether staff receive any guidance about connecting corporate devices to public or unknown open Wi-Fi.
Check whether the organisation itself operates an open guest SSID whose name could be trivially cloned, increasing the pool of devices that will auto-join a look-alike.
Broadcast a benign, clearly-scoped open SSID matching a probed name and count how many devices auto-associate without any user interaction over a fixed observation window.
Correlate associating client MAC OUIs against the known corporate device fleet to distinguish employee-owned phones from managed corporate endpoints.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the engagement authorises broadcasting a look-alike open SSID and observing real staff devices, and agree the physical location and observation window with the client.
From the passive capture, choose an SSID name that multiple staff devices are probing for, or clone the organisation's own open guest SSID name.
Stand up an open (no-encryption) rogue AP with that SSID using hostapd-mana, ensuring it does not forward to the internet unless the client explicitly authorises full interception.
Log each associating client's MAC, signal strength, and timestamp, and note how many joined with zero user interaction versus tapping a prompt.
For authorised proof-of-concept only, present a benign captive splash page recording that the device reached attacker-controlled web content, without harvesting any real credential.

Tear down the rogue AP at the end of the window and report aggregate association counts and the split between corporate and personal devices, not individual employee identities unless the client requests it.

variants: Karma/MANA-style responding, where the rogue AP answers every probe request with the requested SSID so it captures devices searching for many different saved open networks at once.
Cloning the organisation's own open guest SSID specifically, so corporate visitors and staff who use guest Wi-Fi are drawn in with a genuinely familiar name.
Targeting a specific executive or team by profiling the exact open SSIDs their devices probe for, then broadcasting only those to reduce noise and detection.
Combining the auto-join with a captive-portal credential prompt so that devices which join silently are then presented with a phishing login the user does act on.
mitigation: Deliver recurring security-awareness training that specifically teaches staff a familiar network name proves nothing and that corporate devices should use only the enterprise SSID or a VPN.
Use MDM/GPO to remove saved open/public networks from managed devices and disable auto-join for any SSID that is not the corporate enterprise network.
Prefer WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise for corporate access so managed devices refuse to authenticate to an impersonated network, and pin the expected server certificate.
If an open guest network is operated, migrate it to WPA3 with Opportunistic Wireless Encryption or an authenticated captive portal so its name cannot be trivially cloned for silent joins.
Deploy an always-on VPN posture on corporate devices so that even an inadvertent join to an untrusted network does not expose cleartext traffic.
Run periodic internal rogue-AP exercises and feed the association rate back into the awareness programme as a measurable metric.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Phones and laptops are built to reconnect automatically to any network whose name they recognise, and they do it silently, without asking. An attacker only has to broadcast a name your staff's devices already trust — the local coffee shop, a common airport network, or even your own guest Wi-Fi — and those devices will quietly join their equipment instead of yours. The most effective fixes are a mix of teaching people that a familiar name is not proof of anything and configuring company devices so they simply refuse to auto-join anything but your real network. Together these turn a silent, invisible connection into one that never happens.

items.title: Users Approving Rogue Certificate Warnings on WPA2-Enterprise
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and injection, plus EAPHammer or hostapd-wpe to run a rogue WPA2-Enterprise AP presenting an untrusted certificate. The test measures whether users click through the certificate-trust prompt that appears when a device is not pre-configured to pin the real RADIUS certificate. Written authorization must cover broadcasting a rogue enterprise SSID and observing whether nominated test users accept the certificate warning.
items.whatItIs: On WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise networks, a device is supposed to verify the login server's certificate before sending the user's password. When a device is not centrally configured to pin the real certificate, the operating system shows the user a 'do you trust this certificate?' prompt. This test measures how many users simply tap 'Trust' or 'Connect anyway' to get online — which hands their domain credentials straight to an attacker-run fake login server. It is an awareness finding because the technical control (certificate validation) is only as good as the user's decision when the prompt appears.
items.rootCause: Where corporate Wi-Fi profiles are not pushed centrally with the CA and expected server name pinned, the certificate decision is delegated to the end user, who is untrained to evaluate a certificate and strongly motivated to get connected. Users learn to dismiss warnings that stand between them and their email. The organisation has neither removed the decision from users via managed profiles nor trained them on why the prompt matters.
items.impact: A single user who accepts the rogue certificate leaks their domain username and an MSCHAPv2 challenge/response (crackable offline) or, in some inner-method configurations, the cleartext password. Those credentials are frequently reused for VPN, email, and single sign-on, escalating a wireless foothold to full account takeover. Because the fake AP can relay the session to the real network, the user's connection appears to succeed and nothing looks wrong. The likelihood of at least one acceptance across a workforce is high, which is what makes the awareness gap serious.
items.realWorldContext: Certificate-warning click-through is the practical failure mode behind most successful evil-twin enterprise attacks: the cryptography is sound, but users defeat it by tapping 'Trust' to reach their inbox. Red teams routinely report that on networks relying on user-approved PEAP, a rogue AP left running through a lunch period collects a steady stream of domain hashes. The lesson organisations repeatedly relearn is that a security prompt shown to a busy, untrained user is not a control — the fix is to take the decision away from the user entirely by pinning the certificate on managed devices.
stepsToIdentify: Inspect the corporate Wi-Fi profile pushed via MDM/GPO to confirm whether the CA certificate and expected RADIUS server name are pinned, or whether certificate trust is left to the user at connection time.
Determine whether the inner EAP method is PEAP-MSCHAPv2 or EAP-TTLS (user-password based, high value) versus EAP-TLS (mutual certificate, not vulnerable to this specific click-through).
Identify BYOD and legacy devices exempt from the managed profile, since these are most likely to present the raw trust prompt to users.
On a test device configured to organisational defaults, associate to a controlled rogue enterprise AP and record whether a certificate-trust dialog appears and what it says.
Interview a sample of staff on what they do when a 'certificate not trusted' prompt appears while joining Wi-Fi, to gauge baseline awareness.
Check whether 802.11w/PMF is enabled, since attackers commonly deauthenticate a target to force the reconnection at which the prompt is shown.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorises a rogue WPA2-Enterprise AP and observation of nominated test users' response to the certificate prompt.
Configure EAPHammer or hostapd-wpe with a self-signed certificate and the cloned corporate SSID and channel.
Broadcast the rogue AP at strong signal and, where authorised, deauthenticate a nominated test client to trigger a reconnection and its certificate prompt.
Record whether the test user accepts the untrusted certificate and, if so, capture the resulting EAP identity and MSCHAPv2 challenge/response as evidence.
Demonstrate crackability by running the captured hash against a representative wordlist within the engagement's time budget, without retaining the recovered credential beyond evidencing.
Tear down the rogue AP, report the acceptance rate among nominated testers, and immediately rotate/report any real (non-test) credential captured incidentally.

examplePayloads.label: Rogue WPA2-Enterprise AP with self-signed cert, credential capture
Legacy rogue RADIUS with certificate the client must trust
Generate a self-signed server certificate for the rogue AP
Force reconnection of a nominated test client to trigger the prompt
Offline-crack a captured MSCHAPv2 challenge/response

variants: EAP-TTLS/PAP inner-method configurations that reveal the cleartext password once the certificate is accepted, removing the offline-cracking step entirely.
Silent-success relay mode, where the rogue AP proxies the accepted session to the real RADIUS server so the user's connection succeeds and no follow-up warning appears.
Targeting BYOD/legacy devices specifically, since they are least likely to have the certificate pinned and most likely to show the user a raw trust prompt.
Fatigue-based repetition, where repeated forced reconnections condition a user to reflexively accept the prompt just to stay online.
mitigation: Push the corporate Wi-Fi profile via MDM/GPO with the CA certificate and expected RADIUS server name pinned, so devices refuse an untrusted certificate silently and never present a user-approvable prompt.
Migrate to EAP-TLS with mutual certificate authentication so there is no user-password to harvest and no click-through decision to make.
Remove BYOD and legacy devices from the enterprise SSID or bring them under the same pinned profile via onboarding tooling (e.g. a provisioning portal).
Train staff specifically that a certificate warning when joining corporate Wi-Fi means stop and report, not connect anyway, and reinforce with periodic simulated exercises.
Enable 802.11w/PMF to make the forced-reconnection precursor harder, reducing how often users are prompted at all.
Deploy WIDS/WIPS that alerts on a rogue AP broadcasting the corporate SSID with a mismatched certificate fingerprint.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your secure staff Wi-Fi is meant to check the identity of the login server before any password is sent. When devices are not centrally set up to do that check automatically, the decision falls to the member of staff, who sees a confusing 'do you trust this certificate?' box and, wanting to get on with their day, taps yes. At that moment their login details go to whoever set up the fake network. The reliable fix is to take the decision away from people: configure company devices so they already know exactly which login server is real and refuse anything else, with no prompt to click. Training that teaches staff to stop and report such a warning is the essential backup for any device that slips through.

items.title: Wi-Fi Password Sharing and Reuse by Staff
items.prerequisites: This is primarily an interview-, observation-, and OSINT-driven awareness assessment rather than a heavy tooling exercise. Useful adjuncts are airodump-ng/hcxdumptool to capture a WPA2-PSK handshake for cracking, and access (with authorization) to shared chat/wiki/ticketing systems where a PSK may have been posted. Written scope should cover reviewing internal collaboration tools and, where a PSK is captured, attempting an offline crack against a representative wordlist.
items.whatItIs: On networks that use a single shared password (WPA2/WPA3-Personal PSK), staff frequently share that password with visitors, contractors, and personal devices, and post it in chat channels, wikis, or sticky notes. The same human habit means the PSK is often a weak, memorable phrase and rarely changed when someone leaves. This test measures how widely the key has spread and how guessable it is — an awareness and process finding about how people handle the one secret protecting the whole network.
items.rootCause: A single pre-shared key has no per-user accountability, so it is treated as a convenience to be passed around rather than a credential to be protected. Staff are not trained to treat the Wi-Fi password like any other secret, and there is usually no process to rotate it after departures or when it leaks. The organisation relies on a secret whose entire security model breaks the moment it is shared once too often.
items.impact: A leaked or guessable PSK gives an attacker full network access from within radio range, indistinguishable from a legitimate user because everyone shares the same key. Former employees, ex-contractors, and anyone who was ever handed the password retain access indefinitely until it is changed. Because the PSK is often posted in searchable internal tools, an attacker who compromises one chat account or finds one exposed wiki can obtain network access without any radio attack at all. The lack of rotation means a single historic leak compromises the network for years.
items.realWorldContext: Shared Wi-Fi passwords are one of the most common quiet weaknesses found on internal engagements: the key is written on a whiteboard in reception, pasted in the 'welcome' channel of a team chat, or the same one used across three office locations for a decade. It is routine to recover the PSK from an internal wiki search before ever touching a radio. The business consequence is that staff turnover silently accumulates people who can still reach the network — a departing contractor who was given the office password can often still connect from the car park months later, and nobody thinks to change it.
stepsToIdentify: Determine whether the network uses WPA2/WPA3-Personal (a single shared PSK) versus Enterprise (per-user credentials), since this finding applies only where a shared key is in use.
With authorization, search internal collaboration tools (chat, wiki, ticketing, shared drives) for the SSID name and terms like 'wifi password' to find where the PSK has been posted.
Interview staff and reception on how the Wi-Fi password is given to visitors and contractors, and whether it is written down anywhere physically visible.
Ask the wireless team when the PSK was last rotated and whether any rotation is triggered by staff or contractor departures.
Capture a WPA2-PSK handshake and attempt an offline crack against a representative wordlist to assess whether the key is weak and memorable (a hallmark of a shared, human-chosen password).
Enumerate how many distinct device types are associated to the PSK network to gauge how far beyond intended users the key has spread.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorises searching internal tools for the PSK and attempting an offline crack of a captured handshake.
Search the organisation's chat/wiki/ticketing systems and shared drives for the SSID and password terms; document any location where the live PSK is exposed.
In parallel, capture a WPA handshake by monitoring the PSK network and, where authorised, sending a targeted deauthentication to a test client to force a reconnection.
Run the captured handshake against a wordlist to confirm whether the key is guessable within the engagement window.
Where the PSK is recovered by either route, demonstrate network access from a controlled test device to prove impact, without pivoting beyond agreed scope.
Report each exposure location and the crack result, and recommend immediate rotation; do not retain the recovered PSK beyond what is needed as evidence.

Force a test client to reconnect and emit a handshake
Offline-crack the captured PSK handshake
GPU-accelerated crack via hashcat (convert then attack WPA mode)
examplePayloads.command: hcxpcapngtool -o psk.hc22000 psk_capture-01.pcapng && hashcat -m 22000 psk.hc22000 wordlist.txt

examplePayloads.label: Search an internal wiki export for a leaked PSK (authorized review)

variants: PSK recovered purely via OSINT/internal search with no radio attack at all, when it has been posted in a searchable internal system.
Physical exposure, where the password is on a sticky note, whiteboard, or laminated card visible to visitors or through a window.
Cross-site key reuse, where the same PSK protects multiple offices so one leak compromises all of them.
Stale key, where a former employee or contractor retains working access because the PSK was never rotated after their departure.
mitigation: Migrate from a shared PSK to WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise (802.1X) so each user has individually revocable credentials and there is no single password to share.
Where a PSK must remain, use a long, random, machine-generated passphrase that is not memorable and therefore not casually shared.
Establish and enforce a rotation process that changes the PSK on a schedule and immediately after any staff or contractor departure or suspected leak.
Provide a separate, isolated guest network with its own credential path (rotating voucher or captive portal) so the corporate PSK is never handed to visitors.
Train staff to treat the Wi-Fi password as a protected secret and never post it in chat, wikis, or on visible notes.
Periodically scan internal collaboration tools for exposed network passwords and remove them.
items.mitigationClientFacing: When a network is protected by a single password that everyone shares, that password inevitably spreads — it gets given to visitors, passed to contractors, written on a whiteboard, and pasted into team chats. Anyone who was ever given it keeps access forever, because there is no way to revoke one person without changing it for everyone, and it rarely gets changed. The strongest fix is to move to a system where each person has their own login that can be switched off when they leave. Short of that, use a long random password nobody can memorise or casually share, change it whenever someone departs, and give visitors a completely separate guest network so your real password never leaves the building.

items.title: Corporate Devices Connected to Untrusted Public Hotspots
items.prerequisites: A rogue-AP toolkit (hostapd-mana or Wifiphisher) to simulate a public hotspot, plus the ability to review MDM/endpoint telemetry for the corporate device fleet. This is a hybrid awareness/configuration test focused on remote and travelling staff. Written authorization must cover simulating a public hotspot that corporate devices may join and reviewing device connection history via MDM.
items.whatItIs: Staff working remotely, travelling, or in coffee shops routinely connect corporate laptops and phones to open public hotspots in airports, hotels, and cafes. These networks are untrusted, frequently impersonated, and expose the device to interception unless a VPN and strong endpoint posture are enforced. This test measures how often corporate devices join such networks and whether protective controls (always-on VPN, DNS-over-HTTPS, firewall posture) actually engage — an awareness and mobile-hygiene finding rather than an attack on the office network itself.
items.rootCause: Remote work spreads corporate devices across networks the organisation does not control, yet staff are seldom trained on the risks of public Wi-Fi and devices are often not configured to protect themselves automatically. Convenience wins: people connect to whatever is available. Without an enforced always-on VPN and endpoint controls, the organisation is trusting each employee to make the right call on every hostile network they encounter.
items.impact: A corporate device on a hostile hotspot exposes traffic to interception, session-token theft, DNS hijacking, and captive-portal phishing while off the corporate perimeter. Cached credentials, internal hostnames, and email sessions can leak, and a device compromised on the road returns to the office network already infected. Because these connections happen away from corporate monitoring, the compromise may go undetected until the device is back inside. The aggregate exposure grows with every travelling or remote employee.
items.realWorldContext: Travelling executives and sales staff are a favourite target precisely because their corporate laptops connect to hotel and airport Wi-Fi that anyone can impersonate. The 'DarkHotel' espionage campaigns famously targeted business travellers via hotel networks, pushing malicious 'updates' to corporate machines. On engagements, reviewing MDM connection history commonly shows corporate laptops that have joined dozens of open public networks with no VPN engaged. The takeaway is that mobile-device awareness and an always-on VPN posture matter as much as anything done to the office WLAN.
stepsToIdentify: Review MDM/endpoint telemetry for the corporate fleet to see how many devices have connection history showing open or public SSIDs (hotel, airport, cafe names).
Check whether an always-on / on-demand VPN is enforced on corporate devices such that traffic is tunnelled the moment any non-corporate network is joined.
Verify endpoint posture on public networks: host firewall enabled, network profile set to public, file/printer sharing disabled, DNS locked to a trusted resolver.
Interview remote and travelling staff on their habits with public Wi-Fi and what guidance, if any, they have received.
Stand up a simulated public hotspot in a controlled area and observe whether corporate test devices join it and whether their VPN and firewall controls engage automatically.
Confirm whether managed devices auto-join open public SSIDs by name (see the auto-join finding) versus requiring explicit user action each time.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorises simulating a public hotspot for corporate test devices and reviewing MDM connection history.
Broadcast an open SSID resembling a common public hotspot name using hostapd-mana in a controlled location, without upstream forwarding unless full interception is authorised.
Join a corporate test device to the simulated hotspot and observe whether the always-on VPN engages before any cleartext traffic leaves the device.
With interception authorised, attempt to observe DNS queries and unencrypted metadata from the test device to demonstrate what a hostile hotspot operator would see when the VPN does not engage.
Present a benign captive-portal splash to confirm the device rendered attacker-controlled content, without harvesting real credentials.
Tear down the hotspot and report which protective controls engaged and which did not, plus aggregate MDM findings on real-world public-network use.

Observe cleartext DNS from a test device on the hotspot (interception authorized)
Serve a benign captive-portal check page
Verify whether the VPN tunnel engaged on the test device (macOS example)
One-shot public-hotspot lure with captive portal

variants: Hotel/airport captive-portal phishing, where the fake network mimics a paid-hotspot login and harvests credentials or payment details.
DarkHotel-style malicious 'update' delivery, where the hostile network prompts a corporate device to install a fake software update.
Split-tunnel VPN weakness, where a misconfigured VPN still leaks DNS or local-subnet traffic to the hostile network.
Personal-hotspot pivot, where staff tether corporate devices through an untrusted phone hotspot that is itself compromised.
mitigation: Enforce an always-on / on-demand VPN on all corporate devices so traffic is tunnelled automatically the instant any network is joined, with no user action required.
Configure endpoint firewalls to treat unknown networks as public, disabling sharing and inbound services, and lock DNS to a trusted resolver (DoH/DoT) to prevent hotspot DNS hijacking.
Train remote and travelling staff on public Wi-Fi risk, including never approving software updates or certificate prompts on untrusted networks.
Use MDM to remove saved public networks and disable auto-join for non-corporate SSIDs so a device never silently rejoins a hostile hotspot.
Provide cellular hotspots or eSIM data to travelling staff so a trusted connection is available and public Wi-Fi is unnecessary.
Monitor MDM connection telemetry for risky public-network use and feed it back into targeted awareness training.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Once a laptop or phone leaves your office it connects to whatever Wi-Fi is around — hotel, airport, or cafe networks that anyone can set up or impersonate. On those networks a stranger can watch or tamper with the device's traffic unless the device protects itself automatically. The dependable fix is to set company devices so that a secure tunnel switches on by itself the moment they join any network, meaning it never matters how trustworthy the Wi-Fi is. Teaching travelling staff to be wary of public Wi-Fi, and never to accept a surprise 'update' or security warning on it, backs that up. Giving frequent travellers a mobile data device removes the temptation entirely.

items.title: No Process for Staff to Report Rogue Access Points
items.prerequisites: This is an awareness- and process-focused assessment combining interviews with a controlled rogue-AP placement to test human detection and reporting. Useful tools are hostapd-mana to run a discreet rogue AP and airodump-ng to confirm its visibility. Written authorization must cover placing a clearly-tagged benign rogue AP in a staff area and observing whether and how staff report it.
items.whatItIs: Even organisations with technical rogue-AP detection often have no route by which an ordinary employee can report a suspicious access point, an unexpected network name, or a device plugged into a network port. This test measures whether staff would notice a rogue AP and, crucially, whether they know how and to whom to report it. Human reporting is frequently the fastest way a physically-planted rogue device is discovered, so the absence of a clear, well-known process is itself a meaningful gap.
items.rootCause: Security-awareness programmes concentrate on phishing and passwords and rarely teach staff what a rogue access point is or that unfamiliar network hardware should be reported. There is often no simple, publicised channel for such a report, so even an observant employee has nowhere to raise it. The organisation implicitly assumes technical controls will catch everything, leaving the human sensor untrained and unheard.
items.impact: A physically-planted rogue AP — a small device connected to a wall port or hidden in an office — can bridge an attacker onto the internal network for weeks if neither technical monitoring nor staff reporting catches it. The longer it goes unreported, the more data it captures and the deeper the foothold becomes. Where technical WIDS is absent, staff reporting is the only detection path, so its absence can mean indefinite dwell time. Rapid human reporting, by contrast, can shut down a planted device within hours.
items.realWorldContext: Planted rogue devices — a cheap AP or a drop-box behind a printer, a Wi-Fi Pineapple in a bag left in a meeting room — are a staple of physical red-team operations precisely because they are rarely reported. On assessments it is common to leave an obvious extra access point in a shared area for a full day and have no one raise it, because staff neither recognise it as suspicious nor know who to tell. The lesson is that a workforce trained to notice and report unfamiliar network hardware, with an easy channel to do so, closes a detection gap that technology alone often misses.
stepsToIdentify: Review the security-awareness curriculum for any content teaching staff what a rogue access point or unauthorised network device looks like and why it matters.
Determine whether a clear, publicised reporting channel exists (a security hotline, ticket type, or email) for suspicious wireless or network hardware, and whether staff know it.
Interview a sample of staff: ask what they would do if they saw an unfamiliar box plugged into a network port or a new unexpected Wi-Fi network in the office.
Check whether the organisation has technical rogue-AP detection (WIDS/WIPS) and, if not, confirm that human reporting is effectively the only detection path.
Place a clearly-tagged benign rogue AP in a staff area (with authorization) and observe over an agreed window whether anyone notices and reports it, and by what route.
Confirm with the security team whether any rogue-AP report has ever actually been received and how it was handled, to test the process end to end.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorises placing a benign, clearly-tagged rogue AP in a staff area and observing the reporting response.
Deploy a small, unobtrusive rogue AP broadcasting an out-of-place SSID in a shared space, tagged internally so it is unmistakably the tester's device if found.
Verify the rogue AP is visible to staff devices with airodump-ng and note its channel, SSID, and signal footprint.
Observe over the agreed window whether any staff member notices the new network or hardware, and whether any report reaches the security team.
Record the time-to-report (if any) and the route it took, and note whether the security team's response process functioned once a report was made.
Remove the rogue AP at the end of the window and report the detection/reporting outcome, framing the finding around the human-reporting gap rather than the device itself.

Minimal config for the tagged test AP
Confirm the rogue AP is visible over the air
Log association attempts to gauge staff-device visibility
Check for any competing WIDS alert that fired instead of a human report

variants: Physical drop-box on a wall port rather than a broadcasting AP, testing whether staff report unexpected hardware plugged into the network.
Meeting-room implant, where a device is left in a shared room to test whether staff question unfamiliar equipment.
Impersonated-SSID variant, where the rogue AP clones the corporate SSID so only a well-trained user would spot the duplicate.
Report-handling failure, where staff do report the device but the security team has no runbook to act on it promptly.
mitigation: Add rogue-AP and unauthorised-hardware awareness to security training so staff recognise unfamiliar network devices and duplicate/unexpected SSIDs as suspicious.
Establish and publicise a simple, low-friction reporting channel (hotline, dedicated ticket type, poster with a QR code) for suspicious wireless or network hardware.
Deploy technical WIDS/WIPS so rogue-AP detection does not depend solely on human observation, and correlate technical alerts with staff reports.
Create an incident-response runbook for rogue-AP reports covering triage, physical location, containment, and removal, and test it periodically.
Run periodic internal rogue-AP exercises and publish the reporting rate as an awareness metric to reinforce the behaviour.
Encourage and recognise staff who report suspicious hardware so the behaviour is positively reinforced rather than treated as a nuisance.
items.mitigationClientFacing: An attacker can plant a small wireless device in your office — behind a printer, in a meeting room, plugged into a spare network socket — and use it as a hidden door into your network. These are rarely spotted by technology alone, so the people in the building are often your best chance of catching one. Yet most staff have never been told what such a device looks like or who to tell if they see one, so a planted box can sit unnoticed for weeks. The fix is inexpensive: teach staff to notice unfamiliar network hardware or unexpected Wi-Fi names, give them a dead-simple way to report it, and make sure someone acts quickly when they do.

items.title: WPS Enabled by Default (PIN Brute-Force / Pixie-Dust)
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and injection, plus the reaver/bully suite and wash for WPS enumeration. WPS attacks are active against the AP's authentication, so written authorization must explicitly cover attempting WPS PIN recovery against in-scope access points. A representative wordlist is not needed — recovery is of the PIN and then the PSK it releases.
items.whatItIs: Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) is a convenience feature, usually on by default, that lets a device join by entering an 8-digit PIN instead of the full password. The PIN's design is fatally weak: it is validated in two halves and the last digit is a checksum, so at most 11,000 guesses recover it, and many chipsets are vulnerable to an offline 'Pixie-Dust' attack that recovers it in seconds. Once the PIN is recovered the AP hands over the actual WPA2 passphrase. This is a configuration-baseline finding: strong WPA2 is undermined entirely by an insecure default feature.
items.rootCause: WPS was designed for ease of setup and ships enabled by default on most consumer and prosumer APs, with a PIN scheme that is mathematically weak and, on many chipsets, generated with insufficient entropy (the Pixie-Dust flaw). Organisations deploy APs without disabling WPS as part of a hardened baseline. The result is that the network's security is set by the weakest enabled feature, not the strongest.
items.impact: Recovering the WPS PIN yields the full WPA2 pre-shared key, giving an attacker complete, persistent network access from radio range. Pixie-Dust makes this near-instant on vulnerable chipsets, and even PIN brute-force is bounded and often lockout-free on older firmware. Because the recovered credential is the actual PSK, changing WPS settings alone is insufficient once it has leaked — the passphrase must be rotated. A strong, well-chosen passphrase provides no protection while WPS remains enabled.
items.realWorldContext: The WPS PIN flaw, disclosed by Stefan Viehböck in 2011 and extended by Dominique Bongard's 2014 Pixie-Dust research, remains one of the most reliable ways into a home or small-office network years later because vendors keep shipping it on by default. On engagements it is common to find branch offices, retail sites, and guest APs with WPS still enabled, allowing PSK recovery in minutes regardless of how strong the passphrase is. The enduring lesson is that a single insecure default feature can nullify an otherwise sound wireless configuration — hardening baselines must explicitly turn WPS off.
stepsToIdentify: Scan for WPS-enabled access points in scope with wash, noting which APs advertise WPS and whether the WPS 'locked' state is set.
For each WPS-enabled AP, record the chipset/vendor from the OUI and information elements to predict Pixie-Dust susceptibility.
Review the organisation's AP hardening baseline to confirm whether disabling WPS is a mandated configuration step and whether it is verified after deployment.
Check whether the AP firmware implements WPS lockout/rate-limiting after failed PIN attempts, which slows but does not stop PIN brute-force.
Confirm whether any 'push-button' (PBC) WPS mode is left active, which can be triggered opportunistically during a maintenance window.
Cross-reference the AP model against known Pixie-Dust-vulnerable chipset lists to prioritise which targets to test.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope explicitly authorises active WPS PIN recovery against the in-scope APs before sending any attempt.
Enumerate WPS-enabled APs with wash and select an unlocked target that the hardening review flagged as WPS-active.
Attempt the offline Pixie-Dust attack first with reaver, since on a vulnerable chipset it recovers the PIN in seconds without online guessing.
If Pixie-Dust fails, fall back to an online PIN brute-force with reaver or bully, respecting any lockout by pacing attempts.
Once the PIN is recovered, capture the WPA2 passphrase that the AP returns and confirm network access from a controlled test device.
Report the recovered PIN and PSK as evidence, recommend immediate WPS disablement and PSK rotation, and do not retain the credentials beyond evidencing.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate WPS-enabled APs and their lock state
Offline Pixie-Dust PIN recovery
Online WPS PIN brute-force (respecting lockout)
Alternative brute-force engine with Pixie-Dust support
Recover the PSK once the correct PIN is known

variants: Pixie-Dust offline attack against chipsets with weak WPS nonce entropy, recovering the PIN without any online guessing.
Online PIN brute-force against firmware without lockout, walking the 11,000-guess space to recovery.
WPS push-button (PBC) hijack, where an attacker triggers association during the brief PBC window if physical or timing access allows.
Null-PIN and known-default-PIN attacks against specific vendor firmware that accepts a fixed or empty PIN.
mitigation: Disable WPS entirely (both PIN and push-button modes) on every access point as a mandatory item in the wireless hardening baseline.
Verify WPS is off after every AP deployment and firmware update, since some updates re-enable it, and audit periodically with wash.
Rotate the WPA2 passphrase on any AP where WPS was ever enabled and reachable, since the PSK may already have been recovered.
Prefer WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise (802.1X) where feasible, removing the shared PSK that WPS would otherwise expose.
Where APs cannot disable WPS, replace them, as an AP that cannot turn off an insecure default should not be in an enterprise baseline.
Use configuration management to push and continuously enforce the WPS-disabled setting across the AP estate to prevent drift.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Many wireless access points ship with a 'quick setup' feature switched on by default that lets a device join using a short numeric code instead of the full password. That code is so weakly designed that an attacker can work it out in minutes — sometimes seconds — and the access point then simply hands over your real Wi-Fi password. This means a long, strong password gives you no protection at all while this feature is on. The fix is straightforward and free: turn the feature off on every access point, confirm it stays off after updates, and change your Wi-Fi password on any device where it was previously enabled, in case the password was already taken.

items.title: Default Access Point / Controller Admin Credentials
items.prerequisites: Network reachability to the AP or wireless-controller management interface (over the air on a management SSID, on the wired management VLAN, or via a discovered admin URL), plus a list of vendor default credentials and a tool such as hydra or a browser for manual login. Written authorization must cover attempting authentication to management interfaces of in-scope wireless infrastructure using default and common credentials.
items.whatItIs: Access points and wireless controllers ship with well-known default administrative credentials (admin/admin, admin/password, vendor-specific defaults). When these are not changed during deployment, anyone who can reach the management interface can log in and take full control of the wireless infrastructure. This test checks whether default or trivially guessable admin credentials remain on in-scope APs and controllers — a configuration-baseline failure that hands over the keys to the entire wireless estate.
items.rootCause: APs and controllers are deployed at scale, sometimes by non-security staff, and the default credential is left in place because changing it is an easy step to skip and there is no enforced baseline verifying it. Vendor defaults are publicly documented, so 'obscure' is not a defence. The organisation trusts each deployment to be hardened by hand rather than enforcing and verifying the change centrally.
items.impact: Administrative access to an AP or controller lets an attacker read or change the WPA2/WPA3 PSK and enterprise settings, create hidden SSIDs, disable logging and PMF, reconfigure VLANs to bridge networks, and push malicious firmware. On a central controller, one default login can compromise every AP it manages across all sites. This is typically rated critical because it is full control of the wireless security posture from a single, publicly-known credential, often reachable without any radio attack at all.
items.realWorldContext: Default credentials on network gear are perennially among the most exploited weaknesses precisely because they require no skill — the Mirai botnet spread across hundreds of thousands of devices largely by trying a short list of factory logins. On internal engagements, reaching a wireless controller's web login and getting in with admin/admin is a common and high-impact finding, often granting control of every AP in the company. The recurring lesson is that changing default credentials and restricting management access is basic hygiene whose omission repeatedly turns a single known password into estate-wide compromise.
stepsToIdentify: Identify wireless management interfaces reachable in scope: AP web UIs, controller GUIs/SSH, and any management SSID, using a port/service scan and vendor fingerprinting.
Determine the AP/controller vendor and model from banners, OUI, and login-page branding to look up documented default credentials.
Attempt login with the vendor's documented default credentials and a short list of common admin/password combinations against a single interface first.
Check whether management interfaces are exposed on the client/data VLAN or a management SSID rather than being restricted to a dedicated, access-controlled management network.
Review the hardening baseline for a mandated credential-change and management-access-restriction step, and whether it is verified post-deployment.
Confirm whether accounts lock out after failed attempts, since absence of lockout enables broader credential testing.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorises attempting default/common credentials against wireless management interfaces before any login attempt.
Enumerate the reachable management interface and identify the vendor/model to select the correct default credential set.
Attempt the documented default login manually in a browser or SSH client against one target, avoiding aggressive automated guessing that could trigger lockout on production gear.
If defaults fail, run a small, paced credential list with hydra against the interface, respecting any lockout policy.

On successful login, evidence the access at read-only depth first (view the PSK/enterprise config and SSID list) before any change, and make no configuration modifications unless explicitly authorised.
Report the working credential and reachable interface, recommend immediate credential rotation and management-plane isolation, and log out without altering the device.

examplePayloads.label: Discover AP/controller management services
Try a documented default login on the web UI
Paced HTTP-form credential test (respecting lockout)
Try default SSH credentials on an AP/controller
Read the running config to evidence PSK/SSID exposure (post-login, read-only)

variants: Central-controller compromise, where one default login on a WLC or cloud-managed controller yields control of every managed AP across all sites.
Undocumented vendor/service accounts left enabled alongside the changed admin account (see the vendor-backdoor finding).
Management interface exposed on the data VLAN or a broadcast management SSID, reachable from the wireless side without wired access.
Default SNMP community strings (public/private) on the same gear, granting read or write access to configuration via SNMP.
mitigation: Change all default administrative credentials on every AP and controller during deployment, using unique strong passwords managed in a vault, and enforce this as a verified baseline step.
Restrict management interfaces to a dedicated, access-controlled management VLAN/network, never reachable from the client/data VLAN or a broadcast SSID.
Disable or rename unused default and service accounts, and require multi-factor authentication for administrative access where the platform supports it.
Use centralised configuration management to push and continuously verify that no default credential or default SNMP community remains anywhere in the estate.
Enable account lockout and administrative-login alerting so credential guessing is slowed and detected.
Audit the AP/controller estate periodically against the current vendor default-credential lists to catch newly-added or reset devices.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Wireless access points and their controllers come from the factory with a standard login — often something as simple as 'admin' and 'admin' — which is published openly for every model. If that login is not changed when the equipment is installed, anyone who can reach its control panel can take full command of your wireless network: read or change your Wi-Fi password, create hidden networks, or switch off your own monitoring. On a central controller, one such login can control every access point across all your sites. The fix is basic and essential: give every device a unique, strong administrator password stored in a password vault, and make sure the control panels can only be reached from a protected management network, never from ordinary Wi-Fi.

links: MITRE ATT&CK T1078.001 (Valid Accounts: Default Accounts)

items.title: Legacy Cipher Suites Still Enabled (TKIP / WPA-TKIP)
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter in monitor mode and the aircrack-ng suite for passive capture and beacon inspection; no active exploitation of the cipher itself is generally required to evidence the finding. Written authorization should cover passive survey of in-scope SSIDs and inspection of their advertised cipher suites, plus any authorized handshake capture.
items.whatItIs: Access points can advertise multiple cipher suites for backward compatibility. When the deprecated TKIP cipher (WPA-TKIP) is left enabled alongside or instead of CCMP/AES, the network's effective security drops to that of the weakest offered cipher. TKIP has known cryptographic weaknesses and its continued presence also forces the AP to disable 802.11n/ac high-throughput rates. This is a configuration-baseline finding: an obsolete algorithm left enabled for compatibility undermines an otherwise modern deployment.
items.rootCause: APs default to mixed-mode (WPA/WPA2 with TKIP+CCMP) to support the oldest possible clients, and administrators leave it that way to avoid breaking a handful of legacy devices. Hardening baselines often fail to mandate CCMP-only (or WPA3-SAE) configuration. The organisation trades measurable security for compatibility with hardware that should have been retired.
items.impact: TKIP is vulnerable to known attacks (Beck-Tews / Ohigashi-Morii) that allow limited packet injection and decryption of short packets such as ARP, and it weakens the overall handshake and QoS security. Its presence signals a network built for legacy compatibility, often correlating with other weak settings. Practically, enabling TKIP also caps the network at legacy 802.11g speeds, so there is a performance cost alongside the security one. The finding is usually medium because full key recovery is not trivial, but it removes headroom the modern cipher provides.
items.realWorldContext: TKIP was a stop-gap meant to bridge WEP to AES-CCMP, and the Wi-Fi Alliance formally deprecated it years ago, yet mixed-mode WPA/WPA2-TKIP configurations linger in retail, hospitality, and older office deployments because one ancient handheld scanner still needs it. On surveys, spotting TKIP in the beacon is a quick tell that the network's baseline has not been refreshed, and it frequently sits alongside other legacy weaknesses. The lesson is that keeping a broken cipher alive 'just for compatibility' quietly holds the whole network to the security of its oldest device.
stepsToIdentify: Run a passive survey with airodump-ng and record the advertised cipher and authentication suites for each in-scope SSID (look for TKIP in the CIPHER column).
Inspect beacon/probe-response RSN and WPA information elements in a capture to confirm whether TKIP is offered alone or in mixed mode with CCMP.
Identify which SSIDs are WPA (original) versus WPA2/WPA3 and whether any still permit WPA-TKIP for legacy client support.
Review the AP/controller configuration and hardening baseline for the mandated cipher policy (CCMP-only / WPA3-SAE) and whether TKIP is explicitly disabled.
Determine which legacy client devices, if any, actually require TKIP, since that dependency drives the remediation path.
Note whether enabling TKIP has forced the AP to disable 802.11n/ac rates, evidencing the performance impact alongside the security one.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorises passive survey and any handshake capture against the in-scope SSIDs.
Capture beacons and, where authorised, a handshake for a TKIP-enabled SSID, and document the exact cipher/auth suites advertised.
Evidence the finding primarily by demonstrating the advertised TKIP support, since the configuration weakness is provable without a full cryptographic break.
Where the client wants a demonstrated attack and it is authorised, describe/attempt the Beck-Tews class limitation (short-packet injection/decryption) against a lab or test client only.
Correlate TKIP presence with the disabled high-throughput rates to quantify the performance and security cost together.
Report the cipher configuration, the legacy client dependency (if any), and the recommended CCMP-only/WPA3 baseline, retaining only capture metadata as evidence.

examplePayloads.label: Passive survey showing advertised cipher suites
Inspect RSN/WPA cipher IEs in a capture
examplePayloads.command: tshark -r cipher_survey-01.cap -Y 'wlan.rsn.pcs.type || wlan.wfa.ie.wpa.mcs.type' -T fields -e wlan.ssid -e wlan.rsn.pcs.type -e wlan.rsn.akms.type

examplePayloads.label: Filter beacons that advertise TKIP (type 2)
Show configured cipher policy on the controller (read-only)

variants: WPA (original) with TKIP only, the weakest still-deployed configuration, more exposed than mixed-mode WPA2.
Mixed-mode WPA2 offering TKIP+CCMP, where a downgrade-capable client or attacker can push toward the weaker cipher.
Group-cipher downgrade, where the multicast/broadcast group cipher remains TKIP even when the pairwise cipher is CCMP, dragging security down for group frames.
Beck-Tews / Ohigashi-Morii short-packet injection against TKIP QoS channels as a demonstrated (lab) attack on the cipher itself.
mitigation: Configure all SSIDs for CCMP (AES) only, disabling TKIP entirely in both pairwise and group cipher settings, as a mandated hardening baseline.
Move to WPA3-SAE (or WPA2/WPA3 transition mode with CCMP) to gain modern cryptographic protections and forward secrecy.
Identify and retire or segment the legacy devices that require TKIP onto an isolated, tightly-scoped SSID rather than weakening the main network.
Ensure the group/multicast cipher is also CCMP, since a TKIP group cipher weakens broadcast frames even with an AES pairwise cipher.
Use configuration management to enforce the CCMP-only policy across the estate and detect any AP that reverts to a mixed-mode default.
Verify the cipher policy after firmware updates, which occasionally reset cipher settings to permissive defaults.
items.mitigationClientFacing: To stay compatible with very old devices, wireless equipment can be set to accept an outdated scrambling method called TKIP alongside the modern one. The problem is that a network is only as strong as the weakest method it accepts, and TKIP has known flaws and also drags your Wi-Fi down to old, slow speeds. In practice it is kept on to support one or two ageing devices, at a cost to everyone else. The fix is to switch every network to the modern method only, and where a genuinely old device still needs the outdated one, put just that device on its own separate, isolated network rather than weakening the main one for all.

links: CWE-327 (Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm)

items.title: 802.11w Protected Management Frames Disabled
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter capable of monitor mode and injection, plus the aircrack-ng suite (aireplay-ng) or mdk4 to test deauthentication susceptibility, and airodump-ng to inspect the RSN capabilities for PMF status. Written authorization must cover sending deauthentication frames to a nominated test client to demonstrate the lack of management-frame protection.
items.whatItIs: 802.11w (Protected Management Frames, PMF) cryptographically protects certain management frames — notably deauthentication and disassociation — so an attacker cannot forge them. When PMF is disabled (the common default on WPA2-Personal), anyone can spoof a deauthentication frame and knock clients off the network at will. That kick is the enabling first step for evil-twin, handshake-capture, and denial-of-service attacks. This is a configuration-baseline finding: a protective standard exists and is simply not turned on.
items.rootCause: PMF was optional under WPA2 and defaults to off on many WPA2-Personal deployments; it is mandatory only under WPA3. Administrators leave it disabled to avoid compatibility issues with older clients, and hardening baselines often omit it. The management frames that control association therefore remain forgeable, exactly as they were in the original standard.
items.impact: Without PMF, an attacker can continuously deauthenticate clients (targeted or broadcast), causing denial of service and, more importantly, forcing reconnections that enable WPA handshake capture for offline PSK cracking and reassociation to an evil-twin AP for credential theft. It is the low-cost precursor that makes several higher-severity wireless attacks reliable. The attack requires no credentials and only radio proximity, so the barrier is minimal. Rated medium as a standalone gap, it amplifies the severity of the attacks it enables.
items.realWorldContext: The forgeable deauthentication frame is the single most abused primitive in Wi-Fi attacks: nearly every 'capture a handshake' or 'kick a client to the evil twin' walkthrough starts with aireplay-ng --deauth precisely because PMF is so often off. 802.11w has existed since 2009 and is mandatory in WPA3, yet WPA2-Personal networks routinely ship with it disabled. The practical lesson is that enabling PMF removes the free first move from a whole family of wireless attacks, turning reliable client-kicks into something an attacker can no longer simply forge.
stepsToIdentify: Inspect the RSN capabilities in beacon/probe-response frames with airodump-ng or tshark to determine each SSID's PMF status: disabled, capable (optional), or required.
Confirm whether the network is WPA2-Personal (PMF commonly off) versus WPA3 (PMF mandatory) versus WPA2-Enterprise (PMF often configurable).
Review the AP/controller configuration and hardening baseline for whether PMF is set to 'required' or at least 'capable' across SSIDs.
Send a controlled deauthentication to a nominated test client and observe whether it is disconnected, confirming the frames are unprotected.
Check whether legacy clients that cannot support PMF exist, since their presence is the usual reason PMF is left disabled.
Note whether the network relies on any WIDS to detect deauthentication floods as a compensating (detective, not preventive) control.
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorises sending deauthentication frames to a nominated test client to evidence the missing protection.
Identify the target SSID/BSSID and confirm from the RSN capabilities that PMF is not required.
Send a small, targeted deauthentication burst to the nominated test client and observe its disconnection as proof the management frames are forgeable.
Demonstrate the downstream value by capturing the WPA handshake produced when the test client reconnects (on a PSK network) or by noting that reassociation to an evil twin would now be possible.
Optionally show a broadcast deauthentication's denial-of-service effect against test devices only, keeping the burst minimal and time-boxed.
Report the PMF status and demonstrated deauthentication, recommend enabling PMF as required, and stop transmitting immediately after evidencing.

examplePayloads.label: Inspect PMF/MFP status from RSN capabilities
examplePayloads.command: tshark -r survey-01.cap -Y 'wlan.rsn.capabilities.mfpc==1 || wlan.rsn.capabilities.mfpr==1' -T fields -e wlan.ssid -e wlan.rsn.capabilities.mfpr -e wlan.rsn.capabilities.mfpc

examplePayloads.label: Targeted deauthentication of a nominated test client
Capture the handshake emitted on reconnection
