Broadcast deauthentication DoS demonstration (test devices only, time-boxed)
Show the WLAN PMF setting on the controller (read-only)
examplePayloads.command: ssh admin@<controller-ip> 'show wlan <wlan-id> | include Management Frame Protection|PMF|11w'

variants: Handshake-capture enablement, where the deauthentication is used purely to force a reconnection and grab the WPA handshake for offline cracking.
Evil-twin reassociation, where the client is kicked off the legitimate AP to draw it onto an attacker-controlled AP.
Broadcast deauthentication denial-of-service against all clients on a cell, causing sustained wireless outage.
Disassociation-frame attacks and CTS/RTS abuse as related unprotected-management-frame techniques PMF also mitigates.
mitigation: Enable 802.11w PMF as 'required' on all WPA2/WPA3 SSIDs where client support allows, and at minimum 'capable' where a mix of clients exists.
Migrate to WPA3, which makes PMF mandatory and removes the option to disable it.
Identify and upgrade or segment the legacy clients that cannot support PMF, rather than leaving it off for the whole network.
Deploy WIDS/WIPS to detect deauthentication/disassociation floods as a detective control alongside the preventive PMF setting.
Use configuration management to enforce the PMF policy across the estate and detect APs that revert to PMF-disabled defaults.
Verify PMF status after firmware updates and new AP deployments as a standard baseline check.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Some of the invisible 'housekeeping' messages that Wi-Fi uses to manage connections — including the message that tells a device to disconnect — are, by default, unprotected and can be forged by anyone nearby. An attacker uses this to repeatedly kick your devices off the network, which is both disruptive in itself and the opening move for stealing passwords or luring devices onto a fake network. A standard feature exists to protect these messages so they can no longer be forged; it is simply often left switched off. Turning it on across your networks, and moving to the newer WPA3 standard where it is always on, removes the attacker's easiest first step.

links: MITRE ATT&CK T1498 (Network Denial of Service)

items.title: Access Point Configuration Drift Across the Estate
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter in monitor mode for over-the-air survey and, where authorized, read access to the wireless controller or individual AP configurations to compare them against the intended baseline. This is a configuration-consistency assessment across many APs. Written authorization should cover surveying all in-scope APs and reviewing their configurations for drift from the documented standard.
items.whatItIs: In a multi-AP estate, individual access points frequently drift from the intended secure baseline: one AP still allows TKIP, another has PMF off, a third broadcasts an old test SSID, a fourth runs older firmware or a weaker cipher after a manual change. This test looks for that inconsistency across the fleet, because attackers seek out the single weakest AP rather than the average. It is a configuration-management finding about the absence of enforced, verified consistency.
items.rootCause: APs are configured and updated over time by different people, through manual changes, partial rollouts, and firmware updates that reset settings, without a central configuration-management system that pushes and continuously verifies one baseline. Drift accumulates silently because each AP looks fine in isolation. The organisation manages APs individually rather than as a governed fleet, so exceptions never get reconciled.
items.impact: An attacker only needs the weakest AP: one node with TKIP, WPS, PMF-off, an open test SSID, or vulnerable firmware provides the same network access as compromising the whole estate. Drift also undermines assurance — a clean audit of a sample AP says nothing about the outliers. Because the weak AP may be in a low-traffic location, the exposure can persist unnoticed for a long time. The finding's severity tracks the worst configuration found across the fleet.
items.realWorldContext: Configuration drift is the quiet reason 'we hardened our Wi-Fi' engagements still yield findings: the flagship office APs are pristine, but a forgotten AP in a warehouse mezzanine or a branch closet still runs the 2019 baseline with WPS on. Attackers and auditors alike home in on that single outlier. On surveys, walking the whole footprint and diffing every AP against the standard routinely surfaces one or two nodes that never got the update. The lesson is that wireless security is set by the weakest access point, so consistency must be enforced and verified by tooling, not assumed from a representative sample.
stepsToIdentify: Survey the entire in-scope footprint with airodump-ng/Kismet, cataloguing every BSSID, its SSID(s), advertised cipher, auth type, and PMF status, including APs in peripheral locations.
Compare each AP's over-the-air advertised settings against the documented secure baseline and flag any deviation (TKIP present, PMF off, WPS on, unexpected SSID).
Where authorised, pull per-AP configuration and firmware version from the controller and diff them against the intended standard to catch drift not visible over the air.
Identify orphaned or legacy SSIDs still broadcast by some APs (old test networks, decommissioned guest SSIDs) that widen the attack surface.
Check whether a central configuration-management/templating system exists and whether it continuously verifies compliance or only applies settings at provisioning time.
Correlate firmware versions across the fleet to find APs lagging behind the current approved image (links to the firmware-patching finding).
exploitationSteps: Confirm scope authorises a full-footprint survey and, where included, read access to AP/controller configurations.
Perform the over-the-air survey across all locations and build a per-AP settings matrix, ranking APs by how far they deviate from the baseline.

Select the weakest AP identified (for example one still offering TKIP or with WPS enabled) and, within its own finding's authorised scope, demonstrate that it provides network access despite the rest of the estate being hardened.
Where config read access is available, evidence the drift precisely by diffing the outlier's configuration and firmware against the standard.
Show that a sample-based audit would have missed the outlier by contrasting the compliant flagship APs with the deviating one.
Report the full drift matrix, the worst-case AP, and the absence of enforced consistency, recommending centralised configuration management.

examplePayloads.label: Full-footprint survey capturing per-AP settings
Build a per-AP cipher/PMF/auth matrix from the capture
examplePayloads.command: tshark -r estate_survey-01.cap -Y 'wlan.fc.type_subtype==0x08' -T fields -e wlan.bssid -e wlan.ssid -e wlan.rsn.pcs.type -e wlan.rsn.capabilities.mfpr | sort -u

examplePayloads.label: Diff a live AP config against the intended baseline (read-only)
examplePayloads.command: ssh admin@<controller-ip> 'show ap config general <ap-name>' > ap.cfg && diff baseline.cfg ap.cfg

examplePayloads.label: List firmware versions across the AP fleet
Enumerate all SSIDs currently broadcast to find orphaned networks

variants: Firmware drift, where a subset of APs run older, vulnerable images the rest of the fleet has moved past.
Orphaned SSID drift, where decommissioned or test SSIDs are still broadcast by a handful of APs, widening the attack surface.
Cipher/PMF drift, where individual APs revert to TKIP or PMF-off after a manual change or update while others stay hardened.
Branch/remote-site drift, where peripheral locations lag the corporate standard because they are updated less frequently.
mitigation: Adopt a centralised wireless controller or configuration-management/templating system that pushes one baseline to every AP and continuously verifies compliance.
Define and document the intended secure baseline (cipher, PMF, WPS-off, SSID list, firmware) and audit the whole fleet against it, not a sample.
Alert on any AP that deviates from the template so drift is caught and reconciled promptly rather than accumulating.
Retire orphaned and test SSIDs, and standardise the broadcast SSID set across all APs.
Re-verify configuration after every firmware update, since updates can reset settings to permissive defaults.
Schedule periodic full-footprint surveys, including peripheral and branch locations, to detect drift that a controller inventory alone might miss.
items.mitigationClientFacing: When you have many wireless access points, they tend to drift apart over time — one gets a manual tweak, another is missed during an update, a third still broadcasts an old test network. Each looks fine on its own, but an attacker only needs to find the single weakest one to get the same access as breaking into the whole system, and it is often a forgotten unit in a back office. Checking just a few 'representative' access points will not catch these strays. The fix is to manage all your access points from one central system that applies the same secure settings everywhere and continuously flags any that fall out of line, so the whole estate stays consistent rather than only the parts you happen to look at.

links: MITRE ATT&CK T1590 (Gather Victim Network Information)
CWE-1188 (Initialization of a Resource with an Insecure Default)

items.title: Pre-Shared Key Printed and Physically Posted
items.prerequisites: Physical or photographic access to areas where the WLAN PSK may be displayed (reception, meeting rooms, break rooms, printed onboarding packs). A camera. Authorization to photograph premises and record any exposed credentials.
items.whatItIs: Many offices write the Wi-Fi password on a whiteboard, a laminated card at reception, or a printed 'welcome' sheet so guests and staff can connect easily. That same key is often the only thing protecting a WPA2-Personal network, so anyone who can see or photograph it — a visitor, a delivery driver, a cleaner — gains lasting access to the wireless network. This test checks whether the PSK is exposed on physical media anywhere it should not be.
items.rootCause: Convenience wins over security: a single shared key is easy to post and hard to rotate, so it gets written down and left visible. Nobody treats the printed key as sensitive media that needs controlled storage and disposal, and WPA2-Personal gives every holder equal, unlogged access.
items.impact: A photographed PSK grants network access that persists until the key is rotated — which, for a posted key, is rarely. An attacker who captures it can join from the car park, decrypt other users' traffic if they also captured the handshake, and pivot to internal systems, all without ever touching a keyboard on-site.
items.realWorldContext: Assessors routinely walk into a lobby for a 'meeting' and photograph the guest — and sometimes the corporate — Wi-Fi key off a reception card or a sticky note on a monitor. Because WPA2-Personal keys are almost never rotated, a key harvested during a single visit frequently still works months later, turning a five-second phone photo into long-term wireless access.
stepsToIdentify: Walk authorized areas (reception, meeting rooms, break rooms, near printers) and note any displayed network names and keys.
Photograph any laminated cards, whiteboards, or printed onboarding material that carry a WLAN key.
Check whether the exposed key is for a guest SSID only or for a corporate/internal SSID.
Attempt to associate to the named SSID using the observed key from outside the controlled area (e.g. the car park) to confirm it is live.
Ask reception staff (as part of an authorized pretext, if in scope) whether they will simply read out the Wi-Fi key on request.
Review whether the same key appears in printed documents left in unlocked drawers or recycling.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the engagement authorizes photographing premises and recording exposed credentials.
Photograph the posted PSK and record its exact SSID and location.
From outside the controlled space, associate to the SSID with the captured key using the OS Wi-Fi client or wpa_supplicant.
Capture a WPA2 4-way handshake for the SSID with airodump-ng to demonstrate that, with the known PSK, any prior-captured traffic for associated clients can be decrypted.
Decrypt a sample capture in Wireshark using the known PSK to prove traffic exposure.
Document how long the key has evidently been posted (dust, lamination wear, onboarding-pack dates) to argue it has never been rotated.

examplePayloads.label: Associate using the captured PSK
Capture a handshake to prove decryptability
Decrypt captured traffic with the known key (tshark)
Confirm the SSID is reachable from outside

variants: Guest key posted publicly but corporate key posted in a staff-only area (still exposed media).
Key distributed in a printed onboarding pack that ends up in recycling (links to MP disposal).
QR-code 'join Wi-Fi' poster that encodes the PSK — same exposure, machine-readable.
Reception staff verbally disclosing the key on request (overlaps AT awareness).
mitigation: Move guest access to a captive portal with per-user or time-limited credentials instead of a shared posted key.
For corporate wireless, use WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise (802.1X) so there is no shared key to post.
Treat any printed key as controlled media: store it out of public sight and shred on disposal.
Rotate any PSK that has been publicly displayed, and rotate on a schedule thereafter.
Train reception and staff never to display or read out network keys.
Use a separate, isolated guest VLAN so an exposed guest key grants no internal access.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your Wi-Fi password is being shown where visitors can see or photograph it — for example on a card at reception or a whiteboard. Because a single password protects the whole wireless network, anyone who captures it can get on the network later, even from the car park, and it is rarely changed. The fix is to stop displaying the password: give guests short-lived logins through a sign-in page, use per-user logins for staff, keep any printed key out of sight, and change any password that has been on display.

items.title: WLAN Keys and Certificates Left on Decommissioned Access Points
items.prerequisites: Physical access to decommissioned, spare, or returned AP hardware (storeroom, e-waste, resale). A serial console cable or the ability to extract firmware/NVRAM. Authorization to inspect and extract configuration from retired devices.
items.whatItIs: When access points are replaced or returned, their stored configuration — including WPA2 pre-shared keys, RADIUS shared secrets, 802.1X certificates, and admin passwords — often stays in the device's flash memory. If those units are resold, sent to e-waste, or left in a storeroom without being wiped, anyone who obtains one can read out the credentials and use them against the still-live network. This test checks whether retired wireless media is properly sanitized.
items.rootCause: Decommissioning focuses on removing the device from service, not on scrubbing its stored secrets. NVRAM/flash retains the last running config unless explicitly erased, and there is often no sanitization step in the disposal process, so credentials ride out of the building inside the hardware.
items.impact: Recovered RADIUS secrets and PSKs can let an attacker impersonate the authentication server, join the enterprise WLAN, or decrypt captured traffic. Extracted 802.1X certificates may still be trusted by clients, enabling a convincing evil-twin. One un-wiped AP from a skip can therefore hand over enterprise wireless access.
items.realWorldContext: Researchers buying used enterprise networking gear on auction sites have repeatedly recovered live VPN keys, RADIUS secrets and Wi-Fi credentials straight from unwiped flash — the same class of finding that made headlines when used routers were shown to still hold prior owners' corporate access. Retired APs are a soft, overlooked source of exactly these secrets.
stepsToIdentify: Inventory decommissioned/spare AP units in scope and their disposal path (storeroom, e-waste, resale).
Connect to a unit's serial console and check whether it boots into a configured state rather than factory defaults.
Dump the running/startup configuration and search for PSKs, RADIUS shared secrets, SNMP strings, and admin hashes.
Extract firmware/NVRAM (e.g. via bootloader, SPI flash reader, or vendor recovery mode) and grep for key material.
Check for stored 802.1X client/server certificates and private keys.
Verify whether any recovered secret still authenticates against the live network.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to inspect and extract configuration from retired hardware.
Console into the retired AP and capture its stored configuration.
Search the config/NVRAM dump for 'psk', 'radius', 'shared-secret', 'certificate', and password fields.
If flash must be read directly, attach an SPI/eMMC reader and image the chip, then carve the filesystem with binwalk.
Extract any RADIUS shared secret and test it by standing up a rogue RADIUS or joining the enterprise SSID with recovered credentials.
Document each recovered secret and whether it remains valid on the production WLAN.

examplePayloads.label: Dump startup config over console
examplePayloads.command: screen /dev/ttyUSB0 9600   # then: show running-config / show startup-config

examplePayloads.label: Image SPI flash
Carve config and keys from the image
Search a text config dump for secrets

variants: Spare/RMA units returned to vendor with config intact.
APs resold on secondary market still holding enterprise certs.
Controller/WLC (not just the AP) decommissioned with the full site config.
Backup config files for the AP left on an unencrypted TFTP/network share (overlaps MP storage).
mitigation: Add a mandatory sanitization step to AP decommissioning: factory-reset and, where supported, crypto-erase before the unit leaves the rack.
Track retired network media through a documented disposal chain with sign-off.
Rotate any RADIUS shared secret, PSK, or certificate that was present on a disposed unit.
Use per-device certificates so a single recovered cert can be revoked without touching the whole fleet.
Physically destroy flash on units that cannot be reliably wiped.
Encrypt configuration backups and restrict access to them.
items.mitigationClientFacing: When you retire or replace a wireless access point, its stored settings — including the Wi-Fi and login passwords and any security certificates — usually stay inside the device. If those units are thrown out, sold, or left in a cupboard without being wiped, someone who gets hold of one can read those secrets and use them to get onto your network. The fix is to always reset and wipe wireless gear before it leaves your control, keep a record of how each device was disposed of, and change any password or certificate that was on a retired unit.

links: MITRE ATT&CK T1552.004 (Unsecured Credentials: Private Keys)

items.title: Pre-Shared Key Distributed Over Insecure Channels
items.prerequisites: Access to the channels the organization uses to share the WLAN key (help-desk tickets, email, chat, shared documents), within an authorized assessment. No wireless hardware strictly required for the disclosure-review part.
items.whatItIs: Organizations frequently hand out the Wi-Fi pre-shared key by emailing it, pasting it into a chat channel, or storing it in a shared document or ticket. Each of those places keeps a lasting, often widely-readable copy of a credential that unlocks the whole wireless network. This test reviews whether the PSK travels and rests on channels where it can be read by people who should not have it.
items.rootCause: A PSK is treated as a low-value convenience string rather than a shared credential, so it is sent over whatever channel is easiest. Those channels retain history, are broadly accessible, and are rarely purged, so the key accumulates copies across mailboxes, chat logs, and documents.
items.impact: Anyone with access to the mailbox, chat archive, or document — including a compromised account, a departed employee, or an over-broad share — obtains lasting wireless access. Because the key is shared, its exposure is unlogged and its rotation is disruptive, so it usually persists.
items.realWorldContext: In assessments it is common to find the corporate Wi-Fi key sitting in a company-wide chat channel or a 'new starter' wiki page that hundreds of people — and every future compromised account — can read. The same key often appears in years of email history, so one mailbox compromise quietly yields network access nobody thinks to revoke.
stepsToIdentify: With authorization, search accessible email, chat (Slack/Teams), and wiki/ticket systems for the WLAN SSID and key.
Identify how widely each location is shared (channel membership, document permissions).
Determine whether the exposed key is for guest or corporate wireless.
Check retention: how far back the key appears and whether old copies are ever purged.
Confirm the discovered key is live by associating to the SSID.
Review the documented process for distributing the key to new joiners.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the assessment authorizes searching internal communication channels.
Search each channel for the SSID name and common key patterns.
Record every location the key was found and the audience size for each.
Associate to the wireless network using a key recovered purely from a communication channel.
Demonstrate that a low-privilege or guest account can reach at least one location holding the key.
Document the exposure breadth and the absence of any rotation tied to staff departures.

examplePayloads.label: Search a mail export for the key
Search chat export
Associate with the recovered key
List who can read a shared doc (example, cloud CLI)
examplePayloads.command: # review sharing scope of the document holding the key, e.g. via the platform's admin/audit UI

variants: Key pinned in a public/company-wide chat channel.
Key in a 'new starter' onboarding wiki page with broad read access.
Key inside a resolved help-desk ticket readable by all agents.
Key in an email thread that auto-forwards to a shared mailbox.
mitigation: Distribute wireless access without a shared secret: use a captive portal (guest) and 802.1X/EAP (corporate).
If a PSK must be shared, deliver it out-of-band and per-recipient, not broadcast to channels with history.
Purge existing copies of the key from chat, email, and documents; restrict who can post credentials.
Rotate the PSK whenever it has been shared broadly or a key-holder leaves.
Apply DLP rules to flag credential-like strings in chat and email.
Move guest onboarding to time-limited, self-service credentials.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your Wi-Fi password is being shared and stored in places like email, chat channels, and shared documents, where lots of people — and anyone who breaks into one account — can read it. Because one password protects the whole wireless network and is rarely changed, every old copy is a way in. The fix is to stop sending the password around: give guests short-lived logins through a sign-in page and give staff individual logins, remove the old copies from chat and email, and change the password if it has been widely shared.

items.title: Sensitive Data Sent in the Clear Over Guest Wireless
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter in monitor mode within range of the guest/open WLAN, and (for open networks) no key at all. For a WPA2-Personal network, the shared key and a captured handshake. Authorization to passively capture wireless traffic.
items.whatItIs: On an open or weakly-protected wireless network, the data moving over the air is a form of media in transit — and if applications on it use unencrypted protocols, that data can be read by anyone listening. This test checks whether staff or guests transmit sensitive information (credentials, internal hostnames, documents) over wireless without transport encryption, so it can be captured off the air.
items.rootCause: Open networks provide no link-layer confidentiality, and WPA2-Personal only protects traffic from those without the key. When applications also skip TLS — legacy internal tools, misconfigured clients, plain HTTP, IMAP/POP without STARTTLS — the payload is exposed in transit over the radio medium.
items.impact: An attacker within radio range can harvest credentials, session cookies, and internal data without touching any wire. On WPA2-Personal, a key-holder who captured the handshake can decrypt other users' sessions. This yields account takeover and internal reconnaissance from a parking spot.
items.realWorldContext: Passive over-the-air capture on open conference and hotel Wi-Fi has produced live credentials for years — the DEF CON 'Wall of Sheep' exists precisely to show attendees their plaintext logins scrolling by. In corporate guest networks, assessors regularly capture internal hostnames and cleartext logins that reveal the internal environment before any active testing begins.
stepsToIdentify: Identify open or WPA2-Personal SSIDs in scope and their client population.
Put the adapter in monitor mode and capture traffic on the target channel.
For open networks, inspect captured frames directly; for WPA2-Personal, decrypt using the known key and a captured handshake.
Search the decrypted traffic for cleartext HTTP, IMAP/POP/SMTP without TLS, FTP, and plaintext credentials.
Flag any internal hostnames, tokens, or documents visible in the clear.
Assess how many client applications fall back to unencrypted transport.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to passively capture wireless traffic on the named SSID.
Enable monitor mode and start a channel-locked capture with airodump-ng.
For WPA2-Personal, capture a 4-way handshake and decrypt the session in Wireshark using the known PSK.
Filter for http, ftp, and non-TLS mail protocols and extract any credentials or sensitive payloads.
Demonstrate reuse of a captured credential or session token against the relevant service (if in scope).
Document each plaintext exposure and the application responsible.

examplePayloads.label: Channel-locked capture
Decrypt WPA2-Personal traffic
Extract cleartext HTTP credentials
Find non-TLS mail logins
examplePayloads.command: tshark -r guestcap-01-dec.cap -Y 'imap || pop || smtp' -T fields -e frame.time -e _ws.col.Info

variants: Cleartext HTTP login on an internal tool reachable from guest Wi-Fi.
Mail client falling back to IMAP without STARTTLS.
Captive-portal itself submitting the guest credential over plain HTTP.
Legacy app using FTP for file transfer over the wireless link.
mitigation: Enforce transport encryption (TLS/STARTTLS/HTTPS) for all applications, with HSTS where applicable.
Use WPA3 or, at minimum, WPA2-Enterprise so per-user keys prevent key-holder decryption.
Isolate the guest network and block it from reaching internal services entirely.
Disable legacy plaintext protocols on the network and on managed clients.
Deploy WIDS to detect monitor-mode capture and rogue APs.
Educate staff not to send sensitive data over guest/open wireless.
items.mitigationClientFacing: On open or shared-password Wi-Fi, anything an app sends without its own encryption can be read by someone nearby listening on the airwaves — passwords, internal system names, even documents. The fix is to make sure every app uses encrypted connections (HTTPS and secure mail), to use per-person Wi-Fi logins instead of one shared password, and to keep guest Wi-Fi walled off from your internal systems so a listener gains nothing useful.

items.title: Wi-Fi Credentials Recoverable from Discarded Printed Media
items.prerequisites: Authorized access to disposal areas (recycling, skips, shredding bins) or discarded printed material. Gloves and a camera. Authorization covering dumpster-diving / discarded-media review as part of the physical assessment.
items.whatItIs: Onboarding sheets, printed network diagrams, and IT run-books frequently contain the wireless key, SSID, and sometimes RADIUS or admin credentials. When those pages are thrown in ordinary recycling rather than shredded, they become recoverable media. This test checks whether wireless credentials leave the building intact on discarded paper.
items.rootCause: Printed operational documents are not treated as sensitive media, so they skip shredding and go into open recycling. There is no disposal control tying 'contains a credential' to 'must be destroyed', so keys ride out on paper.
items.impact: A single recovered onboarding sheet or run-book page can hand over the wireless key — and occasionally the RADIUS secret or AP admin password — enabling network access with no technical attack at all. The exposure is silent and the key is rarely rotated after paper disposal.
items.realWorldContext: Dumpster-diving remains a staple of physical red-team engagements precisely because it works: assessors routinely recover printed Wi-Fi keys, network diagrams and even password lists from unshredded office recycling. It is one of the lowest-effort, highest-signal findings in a physical assessment, and it maps directly to how real intruders gather footholds.
stepsToIdentify: With authorization, review recycling and disposal areas for printed IT/onboarding material.
Photograph any page containing an SSID, key, RADIUS secret, or admin credential.
Determine whether the recovered key is for guest or corporate wireless.
Check whether shredding is available but unused, versus absent entirely.
Confirm the recovered key is live by associating to the SSID.
Review the document-disposal policy and whether it names wireless credentials.
exploitationSteps: Confirm the physical assessment authorizes reviewing discarded media.
Recover and photograph printed pages carrying wireless credentials.
Associate to the wireless network using a key obtained solely from discarded paper.
If a RADIUS secret or admin password was recovered, demonstrate its impact within scope.
Document the disposal location, the audience with access to it, and the absence of shredding.
Correlate the paper's age with the last key rotation to show persistence.

examplePayloads.label: Associate with the recovered key
Test a recovered AP admin login (SSH)
examplePayloads.command: ssh admin@<ap-mgmt-ip>   # using the recovered credential, within scope

examplePayloads.label: Confirm SSID presence
Photograph evidence
examplePayloads.command: # capture the discarded page with visible SSID/key as engagement evidence

variants: Network diagram in recycling exposing SSIDs and segmentation.
IT run-book page with the RADIUS shared secret.
Printed 'guest Wi-Fi' cards discarded in bulk after an event.
Shredder present but bypassed for convenience (policy vs practice gap).
mitigation: Mandate cross-cut shredding for any printed material containing credentials or network detail.
Provide secure disposal bins and remove open recycling for IT documents.
Avoid printing wireless keys at all; use portal/802.1X onboarding instead.
Rotate any key that appears on discarded paper.
Include wireless credentials explicitly in the media-disposal policy.
Audit disposal areas periodically as part of physical security checks.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Printed pages like onboarding sheets and network diagrams often contain the Wi-Fi password, and when they are thrown in normal recycling instead of being shredded, someone can retrieve them and get onto your network with no hacking at all. The fix is to shred anything with a password or network detail on it, provide secure disposal bins, avoid printing Wi-Fi keys in the first place, and change any password that has ended up in the bin.

items.title: Access Point Physically Reachable with Exposed Reset Button
items.prerequisites: Physical access to areas where APs are mounted (open ceilings, walls, desks). Authorization to physically inspect and, where permitted, reset a device. A paperclip / reset tool.
items.whatItIs: Access points mounted within arm's reach — on a desk, low wall, or exposed drop-ceiling tile — can be physically manipulated: pressing the reset button restores factory defaults (default admin password, open management), and the console/Ethernet port may be reachable too. This test checks whether APs are physically protected against tampering.
items.rootCause: APs are placed for radio coverage, not physical security, so they end up reachable. Vendors expose a reset button and often a console port for field service, and nothing physically prevents a passer-by from using them.
items.impact: A factory-reset AP reverts to default credentials and open management, letting an attacker reconfigure it, add a backdoor SSID, or capture traffic. Physical Ethernet access can also grant wired LAN entry behind the wireless controls.
items.realWorldContext: Assessors regularly find enterprise APs sitting on top of ceiling tiles or bolted to a lobby wall at head height, reset button and console port fully exposed. A ten-second factory reset with a paperclip is a classic physical-red-team move that turns a coverage decision into an open door.
stepsToIdentify: Locate in-scope APs and record their mounting height and accessibility.
Note whether the reset button, console port, and Ethernet uplink are physically reachable.
Check for tamper-evident mounting or locked enclosures.
Determine whether a reset would restore default admin credentials (vendor behaviour).
Assess whether the AP's Ethernet drop enforces port security / 802.1X.
Document any AP reachable without tools or keys.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization for physical inspection and any reset action.
Photograph the reachable AP, reset button, and ports.
Where explicitly authorized, perform a factory reset and confirm the AP returns to default management.
Log into the reset AP with vendor default credentials to prove impact.
If the uplink is reachable, test wired access behind the AP for port security.
Restore the AP configuration and document the exposure.

examplePayloads.label: Log into a reset AP (default creds)
examplePayloads.command: ssh admin@<ap-ip>   # vendor default password after reset

examplePayloads.label: Check uplink port security (from a laptop on the AP drop)
examplePayloads.command: nmcli dev connect eth0 && ip a   # did we get a LAN address without 802.1X?

examplePayloads.label: Scan the management interface
Photograph the exposed reset/console
examplePayloads.command: # capture the reachable reset button and console port

variants: Console port reachable for direct configuration extraction.
PoE injector/switch port reachable, giving wired LAN access.
AP in an unlocked comms cupboard rather than a secured rack.
Desk-mounted AP a visitor can simply pocket (device theft).
mitigation: Mount APs out of reach or inside tamper-resistant, lockable enclosures.
Disable or protect the physical reset where the vendor allows; alert on unexpected resets.
Enforce 802.1X/port security on the AP's wired uplink so physical access grants no LAN entry.
Change all default management credentials and store them centrally.
Use tamper-evident seals and inventory checks on deployed APs.
Monitor controllers for APs dropping to default/unmanaged state.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Wi-Fi access points that are within reach — on a low wall, a desk, or a ceiling you can lift — can be tampered with: pressing the reset button returns the device to its factory password and open settings, and the network cable behind it may also be reachable. The fix is to mount access points out of reach or in locked enclosures, make sure the cable they plug into won't grant network access to a stranger, and change all default passwords.

links: NIST SP 800-53 PE-3 Physical Access Control

items.title: RF Coverage Bleeds Beyond the Building Perimeter
items.prerequisites: A wireless adapter and directional antenna, and access to the exterior perimeter (car park, street, neighbouring floor). Authorization to survey signal strength off-premises. A site plan for reference.
items.whatItIs: Wireless signals do not stop at the wall. When AP power and antenna placement push usable coverage well outside the building — into a car park, the street, or a neighbouring tenancy — attackers can conduct every wireless attack (handshake capture, evil-twin, deauth, cracking) from a comfortable, unobserved position. This test measures how far exploitable coverage extends beyond the controlled area.
items.rootCause: APs are often deployed at maximum power for reliability, and antenna choice/placement is rarely tuned to contain the signal. The result is unnecessary coverage bleed that hands attackers a safe operating zone off-premises.
items.impact: External coverage lets an attacker capture WPA2 handshakes and crack PSKs offline, stand up an evil-twin, or jam/deauth from a car — all without entering the building or being seen. It effectively removes physical access as a barrier to wireless attack.
items.realWorldContext: War-driving studies and countless red-team reports show corporate Wi-Fi reliably reachable from the street or car park, giving attackers a patient, unobserved base to capture handshakes and crack offline. Containing RF is a genuine physical-security control that is almost always neglected.
stepsToIdentify: From inside, baseline expected coverage against the site plan.
Walk/drive the exterior perimeter measuring signal strength for each in-scope SSID.
Map where usable (associable / handshake-capturable) coverage extends beyond the controlled boundary.
Identify APs contributing most to the bleed (power, placement, antenna).
Attempt a handshake capture from the furthest external point with usable signal.
Assess neighbouring floors/tenancies for internal bleed as well.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to survey signal off-premises and capture handshakes.
Perform an external RF survey and record RSSI vs. location for each SSID.
From the furthest usable external point, capture a WPA2 handshake to prove exploitability.
Demonstrate offline PSK cracking feasibility on the captured handshake (time-boxed).
Map the external 'attack zone' and identify the responsible APs.
Document containment gaps against the site boundary.

examplePayloads.label: Measure external signal strength
examplePayloads.command: airodump-ng <interface>mon --essid '<SSID>'   # record PWR at each external point

examplePayloads.label: Capture a handshake from outside
Force a handshake with a deauth (if authorized)
Assess crack feasibility

variants: Coverage bleeding to a shared car park an attacker can sit in.
Signal reaching a neighbouring tenant's floor (internal bleed).
High-gain client on the AP allowing capture from further than expected.
Directional attacker antenna extending effective range far beyond casual survey.
mitigation: Tune AP transmit power and antenna placement to contain coverage within the controlled area.
Prefer WPA3-SAE / WPA2-Enterprise so captured handshakes are not offline-crackable to a PSK.
Use directional/down-tilt antennas near the perimeter to reduce bleed.
Deploy WIDS to detect external capture and rogue activity.
Treat the RF perimeter as part of physical security reviews.
Shield or reposition APs adjacent to exterior walls and windows.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Wi-Fi signals travel past your walls, and when they reach the car park or street an attacker can sit outside and attack your network unseen — capturing the data needed to crack the password or setting up a fake network. The fix is to tune the access points so coverage stays inside the building, use stronger Wi-Fi security that can't be cracked offline, and treat how far your signal reaches as part of your physical security.

items.title: Uncontrolled Physical Access to Wireless Controller / PoE Switch
items.prerequisites: Physical access to network cupboards / comms rooms housing the WLAN controller (WLC) or PoE switches. Authorization to physically inspect these areas. A console cable.
items.whatItIs: The wireless LAN controller and the PoE switches feeding the APs concentrate control of the entire wireless estate. If the room or cabinet housing them is unlocked or shared, an attacker with brief physical access can console in, read the full configuration (keys, RADIUS secrets), add a rogue AP, or simply disrupt wireless service. This test checks physical protection of the wireless control plane.
items.rootCause: Comms rooms are often shared with facilities, propped open, or secured only by a common key. The controller/switch console assumes the room is the security boundary, so once inside, access is trivial.
items.impact: Console access to a WLC exposes the whole wireless configuration and lets an attacker provision malicious APs, disable protections, or capture traffic centrally. Access to PoE switches allows AP power/port manipulation and wired pivoting.
items.realWorldContext: Physical red-team engagements repeatedly reach comms rooms left unlocked or propped open, where a single console session against the controller yields site-wide wireless control. The control plane is far more valuable than any one AP, and it is frequently the least physically protected.
stepsToIdentify: Identify where the WLC and PoE switches are located and how the space is secured.
Check for shared keys, propped doors, or tailgating opportunities into the room.
Determine whether the controller console is reachable and whether it prompts for credentials.
Review whether config backups or credentials are also stored in the room.
Assess whether switch ports in the room enforce any access control.
Document the blast radius of controller access.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization for physical access to comms rooms.
Gain (authorized) entry and photograph the controller/switch setup.
Console into the WLC and attempt to view the running configuration.
Extract RADIUS secrets/PSKs from the configuration to demonstrate impact.
Show that a rogue AP could be provisioned or a protection disabled (describe, do not disrupt production).
Document the physical control gaps and the centralized impact.

examplePayloads.label: Console into the controller
examplePayloads.command: screen /dev/ttyUSB0 9600   # then: show run / show wlan

examplePayloads.label: Extract secrets from the config
Enumerate managed APs from the WLC
examplePayloads.command: show ap summary   # inventory of every AP under this controller

examplePayloads.label: Check switch port access control
examplePayloads.command: show port-security   # is any control enforced on these ports?

variants: Shared comms-room key held by facilities/cleaning staff.
Controller reachable over an unauthenticated console.
Config backups stored on a laptop or share in the same room.
PoE switch letting an attacker disable AP power to force client roaming to a rogue AP.
mitigation: Secure comms rooms with dedicated access control, logging, and no shared keys.
Require credentials on all console/management access to controllers and switches.
Alert on controller configuration changes and new AP provisioning.
Store configuration backups encrypted and off-device.
Enforce port security on switch ports even inside the room.
Review physical access to network infrastructure in security audits.
items.mitigationClientFacing: The equipment that controls all your wireless access points sits in a network cupboard. If that room is unlocked or uses a shared key, someone who gets in briefly can take control of the whole wireless network, read its passwords, or add a fake access point. The fix is to properly lock and log access to these rooms, require a login on the equipment itself even for someone standing in front of it, and get alerts when the wireless settings are changed.

links: NIST SP 800-53 PE-3 Physical Access Control

items.title: No Physical Tamper Detection on Deployed Access Points
items.prerequisites: Physical access to deployed APs and, ideally, the monitoring/controller console to check for tamper alerts. Authorization to physically handle an AP and observe whether the action is detected.
items.whatItIs: Even when APs are reasonably placed, organizations rarely detect physical tampering: an AP being unplugged, swapped for a malicious look-alike, or fitted with an inline tap often raises no alert. This test checks whether physical interference with an AP is noticed by monitoring.
items.rootCause: Wireless monitoring focuses on RF and client behaviour, not on the physical integrity of the AP hardware. Controllers may log an AP going offline but treat it as a fault, not a security event, so tampering blends into normal churn.
items.impact: Undetected tampering lets an attacker insert a rogue AP in place of a real one, add an inline network tap, or attach a malicious device to the AP's port — capturing traffic or gaining LAN access while monitoring stays silent.
items.realWorldContext: Rogue-device implants and AP swaps are a known physical-attack technique, and in most environments the only 'detection' is a help-desk ticket when coverage drops. Treating an AP going dark as a mere fault, rather than a possible tamper event, is exactly the blind spot attackers rely on.
stepsToIdentify: Review whether the controller distinguishes an AP fault from possible tampering.
Check for any alerting when an AP goes offline, is replaced, or reboots unexpectedly.
Physically disconnect/replace a test AP (where authorized) and observe whether any security alert fires.
Assess whether a rogue AP presenting the same identity would be detected (WIDS).
Check whether AP uplink ports would detect an inserted tap or new MAC.
Document the detection gaps for physical AP interference.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to physically handle an AP and test detection.
Baseline the monitoring view for the target AP.
Disconnect the AP and observe whether the event is flagged as security-relevant or merely a fault.
Introduce a look-alike/rogue AP with the same SSID/BSSID and check WIDS response.
If authorized, insert an inline device on the AP uplink and check for port/MAC alerts.
Document what interference went undetected and for how long.

examplePayloads.label: Observe controller AP state
examplePayloads.command: show ap summary | include <ap-name>   # fault vs tamper distinction?

examplePayloads.label: Stand up a same-identity rogue AP
examplePayloads.command: hostapd-mana rogue.conf   # does WIDS flag the duplicate BSSID/SSID?

examplePayloads.label: Check for new MAC on the AP uplink port
Time how long an offline AP goes un-alerted
examplePayloads.command: # record interval between disconnect and any security alert

variants: AP swapped for a malicious clone with the same identity.
Inline tap added to the AP's Ethernet uplink.
AP relocated to extend coverage into an attacker area.
Malicious USB/serial device attached to an AP console port.
mitigation: Enable and tune WIDS/WIPS to flag duplicate identities and rogue APs.
Treat unexpected AP offline/reboot events as security-relevant, with alerting.
Enforce port security / 802.1X on AP uplinks to detect new MACs or taps.
Use tamper-evident mounting and periodic physical inventory checks.
Correlate physical access logs with AP state changes.
Alert on APs re-registering with changed hardware identifiers.
items.mitigationClientFacing: If someone unplugs one of your access points, swaps it for a fake one, or attaches a tapping device, most networks don't notice — it just looks like a device fault. The fix is to treat an access point suddenly going offline or changing as a possible security event, use wireless monitoring that spots fake access points, and make the network cable an access point plugs into reject unexpected devices.

links: MITRE ATT&CK T1557.004 (Rogue Wi-Fi Access Points)

items.title: Guest/Public Wireless Enables Attacks from Uncontrolled Areas
items.prerequisites: A device in a public-access area served by the guest WLAN (lobby, waiting room, shared reception). Authorization to test from those public areas. Standard wireless tooling.
items.whatItIs: Guest or public wireless is frequently reachable from lobbies, waiting rooms, and shared spaces that anyone can enter without challenge. That gives an attacker a legitimate, unremarkable physical position from which to run wireless and network attacks. This test checks whether public-area wireless access is properly isolated so that a stranger sitting in the lobby cannot reach anything of value.
items.rootCause: Guest wireless is designed for openness, and it is often available in uncontrolled physical spaces. If it is not strictly isolated, physical openness plus network openness combine into an easy foothold.
items.impact: From a chair in the lobby, an attacker on guest Wi-Fi can scan for internal reachability, capture other guests' traffic, run an evil-twin, or attempt lateral movement if isolation is weak — all while appearing to be an ordinary visitor.
items.realWorldContext: Waiting-room and lobby Wi-Fi is a favourite starting point in physical/wireless assessments precisely because it requires no pretext: the attacker is just a person sitting down. Where guest isolation is weak, that seat becomes a launch point into the internal network.
stepsToIdentify: Identify public-access areas served by guest/public wireless.
From such an area, enumerate what the guest network can reach (internal ranges, management interfaces, other clients).
Test client-to-client isolation on the guest SSID.
Attempt to reach internal services or the wired network from guest Wi-Fi.
Assess whether an evil-twin could be run credibly from the public area.
Document the combination of physical openness and network reach.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to test from public areas.
Associate to the guest network from the public space.
Scan for internal reachability and management interfaces.
Test whether other guest clients are reachable (isolation failure).
Attempt to pivot toward internal/wired resources; stop at proof, not disruption.
Document the reachable attack surface from an uncontrolled seat.

examplePayloads.label: Scan for internal reachability from guest Wi-Fi
Test client-to-client isolation
Probe for management interfaces
Attempt a same-SSID evil twin (if authorized)

variants: Guest network without client isolation, exposing other visitors.
Guest VLAN able to reach internal management interfaces.
Evil-twin of the guest SSID run from the lobby.
Wired jacks in the public area on the same segment as guest Wi-Fi.
mitigation: Strictly isolate guest wireless to an internet-only VLAN with no internal reachability.
Enable client-to-client isolation on the guest SSID.
Deploy WIDS to detect evil-twins in public areas.
Disable or lock down wired jacks in uncontrolled spaces.
Apply firewall egress rules limiting guest traffic to the internet only.
Consider controlling physical access to areas where sensitive wireless is reachable.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Your guest Wi-Fi can be used by anyone sitting in the lobby or waiting room, which gives a stranger a comfortable place to attack from. If that guest network isn't fully separated from your internal systems, they can probe or reach things they shouldn't. The fix is to keep guest Wi-Fi strictly internet-only and walled off from internal systems, stop guests from seeing each other on the network, and watch for fake networks in public areas.

links: MITRE ATT&CK T1557.004 (Rogue Wi-Fi Access Points)

items.title: No Regular Wireless Site Survey or Rogue-AP Sweep
items.prerequisites: Wireless survey tooling (Kismet, Ekahau, or airodump-ng) and authorization to perform an on-site wireless survey. A reference AP inventory to compare against.
items.whatItIs: A wireless environment changes constantly: new APs appear, staff plug in personal routers, neighbours' networks overlap, and attackers can add rogue APs. Without a regular site survey and rogue-AP sweep, none of this is detected. This test checks whether the organization periodically assesses its actual wireless attack surface against its known inventory.
items.rootCause: Wireless is often treated as 'set and forget'. There is no scheduled survey, no maintained AP inventory to diff against, and no ownership for rogue-AP detection, so the real RF picture drifts unseen from the intended one.
items.impact: Undetected rogue and shadow APs create unmonitored entry points; overlapping/mis-tuned APs create coverage bleed; and the organization has no basis to assess wireless risk. Attackers exploit exactly the gaps a survey would reveal.
items.realWorldContext: In assessments it is common to discover employee-installed 'convenience' APs and long-forgotten test SSIDs that no one has surveyed for in years — each an unmonitored door. Regular surveys are how mature programs catch these before an attacker does; their absence is a recurring root cause behind rogue-AP findings.
stepsToIdentify: Ask for evidence of a scheduled wireless site survey and rogue-AP sweep, and their cadence.
Request the current authoritative AP inventory.
Perform a survey and enumerate every SSID/BSSID observed on-site.
Diff observed APs against the inventory to find rogue/shadow/unknown devices.
Identify coverage bleed and channel overlap that a survey would normally flag.
Assess whether any WIDS/WIPS provides continuous rogue detection between surveys.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization for an on-site wireless survey.
Capture all observable APs and clients across the site.
Compare against the AP inventory and flag every device not accounted for.
Investigate each unknown AP (personal router, neighbour, or malicious).
Demonstrate that at least one unaccounted-for AP has gone undetected due to no survey process.
Document the absence of survey cadence and the resulting blind spots.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate all local APs
Long-run passive survey
Diff observed vs inventory
Flag same-SSID different-BSSID (possible rogue)

variants: Employee-installed personal router as a shadow AP.
Forgotten test/lab SSID still broadcasting.
Neighbouring tenant AP overlapping the corporate channel.
Malicious rogue AP that a survey would have caught.
mitigation: Establish a scheduled wireless site survey and rogue-AP sweep with defined cadence and ownership.
Maintain an authoritative AP inventory to diff surveys against.
Deploy continuous WIDS/WIPS for rogue detection between surveys.
Feed survey findings into the organization's risk assessment.
Investigate and remove every unaccounted-for AP.
Track coverage bleed and channel plan as part of the survey.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Wireless networks change all the time — staff plug in their own routers, old test networks linger, and attackers can add fake access points. Without a regular wireless survey, none of this gets noticed. The fix is to schedule routine wireless surveys, keep an up-to-date list of your real access points to compare against, and use continuous monitoring so unexpected or fake networks are spotted between surveys.

items.title: End-of-Life Access Point Firmware Never Risk-Assessed
items.prerequisites: Ability to enumerate AP models and firmware versions (management console or fingerprinting) and authorization to assess them. Vendor EOL/advisory references.
items.whatItIs: Access points reach end-of-life and stop receiving security patches, yet they often keep running for years. If the organization never assesses which APs are unsupported and what known vulnerabilities affect them, it carries unquantified, unpatchable risk. This test checks whether wireless hardware/firmware is included in risk assessment and lifecycle management.
items.rootCause: APs are durable and 'still work', so replacement is deferred. There is no process linking AP models to vendor EOL dates and CVEs, so unsupported devices accumulate without anyone assessing the risk they represent.
items.impact: Unpatched EOL APs may carry known remote vulnerabilities (management RCE, auth bypass, KRACK/FragAttacks-class flaws) that an attacker can exploit for a foothold or persistent rogue infrastructure — and there is no vendor fix.
items.realWorldContext: Networks are full of Wi-Fi gear years past support, and attackers actively target known firmware CVEs in edge devices because they are rarely patched. The absence of any lifecycle/risk assessment for APs is the reason these devices quietly become the softest remote target on the estate.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate AP models and firmware versions across the estate.
Map each model to vendor support status and EOL date.
Cross-reference firmware versions against vendor security advisories/CVEs.
Identify APs that are unsupported or missing critical patches.
Check whether AP lifecycle/firmware is part of any documented risk assessment.
Assess exploitability of the most severe known issues (safely, in scope).
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to assess AP firmware and known vulnerabilities.
Collect model/firmware data from the controller or by fingerprinting.
Build a list of EOL/unsupported APs and their associated CVEs.
For an in-scope, non-disruptive case, validate exploitability of a known management vulnerability.
Show that no risk-assessment process tracked these devices.
Document the unquantified risk and remediation priority.

examplePayloads.label: Fingerprint AP management interface
Pull firmware version from the controller
examplePayloads.command: show ap image all   # model + running firmware per AP

examplePayloads.label: Check advisories for the version
examplePayloads.command: searchsploit <vendor> <model> && # cross-check vendor PSIRT advisories for the firmware

examplePayloads.label: Validate a known mgmt issue (in scope)

variants: EOL AP with a known management-interface RCE.
AP firmware vulnerable to a well-known Wi-Fi flaw with no patch available.
Mixed fleet where only some models are supported (inconsistent risk).
AP whose vendor has exited the market entirely, leaving no patches.
mitigation: Inventory AP models/firmware and map them to vendor EOL and advisories.
Add wireless hardware to the lifecycle and risk-assessment process.
Replace or isolate unsupported APs; prioritize by exploitability.
Subscribe to vendor security advisories and patch on a defined cadence.
Segment legacy APs away from sensitive networks until replaced.
Track a hardware refresh budget/plan tied to EOL dates.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Wi-Fi access points eventually stop getting security updates, but they often keep running for years. If no one checks which ones are out of support and what known weaknesses they have, you're carrying risk you can't fix and don't even know about. The fix is to keep a list of your access points and their support status, check them against the vendor's security notices, and replace or isolate the ones that are no longer supported.

items.title: No Wireless Intrusion Detection to Assess Active Threats
items.prerequisites: Ability to review the organization's wireless monitoring capability, and authorization to run benign wireless events (a controlled deauth or a test rogue SSID) to check for detection. Standard wireless tooling.
items.whatItIs: Wireless attacks — deauthentication floods, rogue APs, evil-twins, handshake capture — leave RF-layer signatures that a Wireless IDS (WIDS) is designed to catch. Without WIDS, the organization cannot assess whether it is under active wireless attack and has no data feeding its risk assessment. This test checks whether wireless threat detection exists and works.
items.rootCause: Wireless monitoring is frequently omitted because the wired IDS/SIEM does not see RF-layer events. With no WIDS, deauths, rogue APs, and captures are simply invisible, so the risk picture is blind to the entire wireless threat surface.
items.impact: Without detection, an attacker can capture handshakes, run evil-twins, and deauth clients repeatedly with no alert, and the organization cannot quantify wireless risk or respond. Detection gaps directly enable the other wireless findings to go unnoticed.
items.realWorldContext: Deauth-based handshake capture and evil-twin attacks are everyday wireless techniques, yet many organizations have no way to see them happening. Assessors routinely run controlled deauths that generate zero alerts, demonstrating that the entire wireless threat surface sits outside the monitoring program.
stepsToIdentify: Review whether any WIDS/WIPS is deployed and integrated into monitoring.
Check whether RF-layer events (deauth, rogue AP, evil-twin) reach the SIEM or a wireless console.
With authorization, generate a controlled deauth and a test rogue SSID.
Observe whether either event produces any alert.
Assess whether wireless threat data feeds the risk assessment at all.
Document the detection coverage (or absence) for each wireless attack class.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to run controlled, benign wireless events for detection testing.
Baseline the monitoring view before testing.
Emit a short, controlled deauth against a test client and check for alerts.
Broadcast a benign test rogue SSID and check for rogue-AP detection.
Correlate with any WIDS/SIEM output to measure detection.
Document which attack classes went entirely undetected.

examplePayloads.label: Controlled deauth (test client, authorized)
Broadcast a benign test rogue SSID
Check for any WIDS event
examplePayloads.command: # review WIDS/WIPS console or SIEM for deauth/rogue-AP alerts in the test window

examplePayloads.label: Confirm handshake capture is silent

variants: Deauth flood undetected (no availability monitoring).
Evil-twin of a corporate SSID raising no alert.
Rogue AP added without detection.
Handshake capture from the perimeter entirely silent.
mitigation: Deploy WIDS/WIPS and integrate its alerts into the SIEM and IR process.
Enable detection for deauth floods, rogue APs, evil-twins, and same-identity duplicates.
Feed wireless threat data into the risk assessment and metrics.
Enable 802.11w (management frame protection) to blunt deauth attacks.
Define response playbooks for wireless alerts.
Periodically test detection with controlled, benign events.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Attacks on Wi-Fi — like knocking devices off the network or setting up fake access points — leave signals that special wireless monitoring can catch, but many organizations have none, so these attacks happen invisibly. The fix is to deploy wireless intrusion detection, connect its alerts to your security monitoring, and turn on Wi-Fi protections that make some of these attacks harder — then test occasionally that the detection actually works.

links: MITRE ATT&CK T1557.004 (Rogue Wi-Fi Access Points)

items.title: Wireless Attack Surface Never Enumerated Against Inventory
items.prerequisites: Wireless survey tooling and an authoritative list of intended SSIDs/APs. Authorization to enumerate the wireless attack surface on-site.
items.whatItIs: The wireless attack surface is the full set of SSIDs, APs, authentication methods, and client behaviours an attacker could target. If it has never been enumerated and compared to what the organization intends to expose, unknown SSIDs, weak auth methods, and legacy configurations persist unassessed. This test checks whether the wireless attack surface is understood and risk-assessed.
items.rootCause: Wireless grows organically — extra SSIDs for events, IoT, or legacy devices — and no one steps back to enumerate the whole surface. Without that enumeration, risk assessment has no accurate input and weak spots hide in plain sight.
items.impact: Unassessed SSIDs may use weak auth (open, WEP, WPA2-PSK) or expose IoT/legacy networks bridged to sensitive systems. Attackers enumerate this surface as their first step; if the defender never has, the attacker knows the environment better than its owner.
items.realWorldContext: The first thing a wireless attacker does is enumerate every SSID and its security — and assessors routinely find event SSIDs, IoT networks and legacy WEP/PSK configurations the owner had forgotten. When the defender has never mapped this surface, they are, quite literally, less informed than the attacker about their own exposure.
stepsToIdentify: Request the intended list of SSIDs, their purpose, and their authentication methods.
Survey the site and enumerate every broadcast (and hidden) SSID and its security.
Compare observed SSIDs/auth against the intended list.
Flag weak methods (open, WEP, WPA2-PSK on sensitive networks) and unknown SSIDs.
Identify IoT/legacy SSIDs and whether they bridge to sensitive segments.
Assess whether this enumeration feeds any risk assessment.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to enumerate the wireless attack surface.
Survey and record every SSID, BSSID, channel, and auth type.
Diff against the intended inventory; flag unknowns and weak auth.
Investigate the purpose and reach of each unaccounted-for or weak SSID.
Show at least one unassessed SSID that presents real risk (weak auth or sensitive bridging).
Document the full surface and the gap versus what was intended.

examplePayloads.label: Enumerate SSIDs and their security
Reveal hidden SSIDs via probe/deauth (authorized)
Classify auth types
Flag weak encryption

variants: Forgotten event SSID still broadcasting with open auth.
IoT SSID on WPA2-PSK bridged toward internal systems.
Legacy WEP network for old hardware.
Hidden SSID assumed safe but trivially revealed and weakly secured.
mitigation: Enumerate the full wireless attack surface and compare it to intended exposure.
Retire unknown, legacy, and weakly-secured SSIDs.
Standardize on WPA3 or WPA2-Enterprise; eliminate WEP and open corporate SSIDs.
Isolate IoT/guest SSIDs from sensitive segments.
Feed the enumerated surface into the risk assessment and re-check periodically.
Document each SSID's purpose, auth, and reach.
items.mitigationClientFacing: The 'wireless attack surface' is every Wi-Fi network you broadcast and how each is secured. If no one has ever mapped this and compared it to what you meant to have, forgotten or weakly-protected networks linger unnoticed — and an attacker will map it before you do. The fix is to survey and list every network you broadcast, remove the ones you don't need, make sure each uses strong security, and review this regularly.

links: MITRE ATT&CK T1016 (System Network Configuration Discovery)

items.title: No Assessment of RF Jamming / Availability Risk
items.prerequisites: A spectrum analyzer or SDR (HackRF/RTL-SDR) and authorization to characterize RF and, where permitted, run a brief controlled interference test in an isolated setting. Do not jam production spectrum without explicit, scoped authorization.
items.whatItIs: Wireless availability can be denied at the RF layer — through deauthentication attacks or raw spectrum jamming — with no need to breach encryption. Organizations that depend on Wi-Fi for critical functions (VoIP, handhelds, IoT, guest services) but never assess this availability risk can be knocked offline. This test checks whether RF availability/jamming risk is understood and mitigated.
items.rootCause: Wi-Fi risk assessments focus on confidentiality (cracking, interception) and rarely on availability. Deauth and jamming are cheap and hard to prevent, yet the dependency on wireless for critical operations is often unquantified.
items.impact: An attacker can deauth clients or jam the spectrum to disable wireless-dependent operations — warehouse scanners, VoIP phones, medical or industrial handhelds — causing operational disruption with minimal skill or equipment.
items.realWorldContext: Deauth floods and cheap SDR jamming are well-documented, and operations that quietly depend on Wi-Fi (scanners, VoIP, IoT) are surprisingly fragile to them. Because availability rarely features in wireless risk assessments, the first time many organizations consider it is during an actual outage.
stepsToIdentify: Identify business functions that depend on wireless availability.
Review whether RF availability/jamming is in the risk assessment at all.
Characterize the RF environment and channel utilization with a spectrum analyzer/SDR.
Assess susceptibility to deauth (is 802.11w enabled?) and to raw jamming.
In an isolated/authorized setting, demonstrate deauth-based denial against a test client.
Document the operational impact of wireless unavailability.
exploitationSteps: Confirm explicit authorization and a safe, isolated setting for any interference test.
Map wireless-dependent operations and their tolerance for outage.
Characterize spectrum usage and identify single points of RF failure.
Demonstrate deauth-based client denial against a test device (802.11w off) in scope.
If authorized and isolated, note raw-jamming susceptibility conceptually rather than in production.
Document the availability risk and mitigations.

examplePayloads.label: Characterize the spectrum
Deauth-based denial (test client, authorized)
Check for 802.11w (management frame protection)
Measure channel congestion

variants: Deauth flood disabling wireless clients (802.11w disabled).
Broadband RF jamming of the 2.4/5GHz band.
Targeted jamming of a critical VoIP/scanner channel.
Congestion-based denial from too many clients on one channel.
mitigation: Include wireless availability and jamming in the risk assessment.
Enable 802.11w (protected management frames) to blunt deauth attacks.
Provide wired fallback for critical wireless-dependent operations.
Deploy WIDS to detect deauth/jamming and alert operations.
Design RF with redundancy and spectrum monitoring for critical areas.
Define an operational response plan for wireless outages.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Wi-Fi can be knocked offline at the radio level — by flooding devices with disconnect messages or jamming the airwaves — without any password-cracking. If your operations depend on Wi-Fi (scanners, phones, IoT) but you've never assessed this, an attacker can disrupt you cheaply. The fix is to include Wi-Fi outages in your risk planning, turn on protections that resist disconnect attacks, provide a wired backup for critical uses, and monitor for interference.

links: MITRE ATT&CK T1498 (Network Denial of Service)

items.title: Consumer-Grade Access Points Used in Enterprise Environment
items.prerequisites: Ability to identify AP make/model (fingerprinting or physical inspection) and authorization to assess them. Vendor documentation on enterprise vs consumer feature sets.
items.whatItIs: Consumer-grade access points bought for convenience or cost lack enterprise security features: no 802.1X/RADIUS, weak management, no central monitoring, and often no timely patching. When they carry corporate traffic, they become the weakest link. This test checks whether wireless hardware was acquired with appropriate security requirements.
items.rootCause: Procurement optimizes for price and speed, and a home router 'works', so consumer gear enters the enterprise without security requirements. Nobody specified enterprise auth, central management, or patch support at acquisition time.
items.impact: Consumer APs typically support only WPA2-PSK, expose weak web management, and lack monitoring — enabling PSK cracking, management compromise, and unmanaged rogue-like behaviour on the corporate network.
items.realWorldContext: Assessors frequently find a home-office-grade router quietly bridging a corporate segment because someone needed coverage fast and procurement had no wireless security standard. That single unmanaged device often offers the easiest wireless foothold on an otherwise well-run estate.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate AP make/model across the environment and classify consumer vs enterprise.
Check which security features each supports (802.1X, central management, monitoring).
Identify consumer APs carrying corporate traffic.
Assess their authentication (likely WPA2-PSK) and management exposure.
Check whether procurement had any wireless security requirements.
Determine patch/support status of the consumer devices.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to assess wireless hardware.
Fingerprint APs and flag consumer-grade models on corporate networks.
Test the weakest security path (e.g. WPA2-PSK handshake capture and offline crack feasibility).
Probe the device's web management for weak/default credentials.
Show the absence of enterprise auth/monitoring and any acquisition requirement.
Document the risk and recommend enterprise-grade replacement.

examplePayloads.label: Fingerprint the AP
Capture and assess a PSK handshake
Test web-mgmt default creds
Check for enterprise auth support

variants: Home router bridging a corporate VLAN.
Consumer AP with WPS enabled by default.
Cheap AP with unpatched web-management RCE.
SOHO mesh gear with no central logging.
mitigation: Define wireless security requirements in procurement (802.1X, central mgmt, patch support).
Replace consumer APs carrying corporate traffic with enterprise-managed hardware.
Move corporate wireless to WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise with RADIUS.
Bring all APs under central management and monitoring.
Prohibit unmanaged/consumer APs on corporate networks via policy and NAC.
Include wireless in the hardware standard and asset inventory.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Cheap home-style Wi-Fi routers used in the office lack the security features business networks need — no per-person logins, weak management, and no central monitoring — so they become the easiest way in. The fix is to set security requirements when buying wireless gear, replace consumer routers with proper enterprise access points, use per-person Wi-Fi logins, and manage and monitor all access points centrally.

items.title: Default or Backdoor Accounts on Wireless Controllers
items.prerequisites: Network reachability to the wireless controller/AP management interface, and authorization to test authentication. Vendor default-credential references.
items.whatItIs: Wireless controllers and managed APs frequently ship with default administrative accounts, and some vendors have included hidden support/backdoor accounts. If these are not removed or changed at acquisition/deployment, an attacker who reaches the management interface gains full control of the wireless estate. This test checks for default and backdoor accounts on wireless management systems.
items.rootCause: Devices ship with working defaults so they can be set up quickly, and acquisition/deployment often skips the step of removing or changing them. Vendor backdoor accounts are undocumented and survive normal hardening.
items.impact: Default/backdoor access to a controller means an attacker can read all wireless secrets, provision rogue APs, disable protections, and monitor traffic centrally — a full compromise of the wireless environment from one login.
items.realWorldContext: Vendor advisories have repeatedly disclosed hardcoded or backdoor accounts in networking and IoT management gear, and default admin logins remain a leading cause of edge-device compromise. Wireless controllers are high-value: one default login can hand over every AP at once.
stepsToIdentify: Enumerate wireless management interfaces (controller, AP web UI, APIs).
Test documented vendor default credentials for the specific model/firmware.
Check vendor advisories for known hidden/backdoor accounts on that firmware.
Assess whether acquisition/deployment mandated credential change and account removal.
Check for weak/reused admin passwords beyond defaults.
Determine the blast radius of controller access.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to test authentication on management interfaces.
Attempt vendor default credentials against the controller/AP management UI/SSH.
Where a firmware is known to carry a backdoor account, test it (in scope, non-disruptive).
On success, demonstrate read of wireless secrets and AP inventory.
Show that no acquisition/deployment process removed or changed these accounts.
Document the finding and full impact.

examplePayloads.label: Test default SSH creds
Test default web login
Check advisories for backdoor accounts
examplePayloads.command: searchsploit <vendor> controller backdoor   # and review vendor PSIRT

examplePayloads.label: Dump secrets after login

variants: Factory default admin/admin never changed.
Undocumented vendor support/backdoor account.
Reused admin password across the whole controller fleet.
Default SNMP community giving read/write to the controller.
mitigation: Require removal/rotation of default and hidden accounts as an acquisition and deployment gate.
Change all management credentials to strong, unique values stored centrally.
Subscribe to vendor advisories and remediate disclosed backdoor accounts promptly.
Restrict management interfaces to an isolated admin network with MFA where supported.
Monitor and alert on management logins.
Include credential hardening in the wireless build standard.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Wi-Fi controllers and access points often come with a default admin password, and some have had hidden 'backdoor' logins. If these aren't removed when the gear is set up, anyone who reaches the management screen can take over your entire wireless network. The fix is to change every default password and remove hidden accounts as a standard setup step, keep management screens on a locked-down network, and watch for admin logins.

items.title: No Security Requirements in Wireless Procurement
items.prerequisites: Access to procurement documentation and wireless build standards (or evidence of their absence), within an authorized review. No wireless hardware strictly required.
items.whatItIs: Whether wireless is secure often depends on decisions made at purchase: does the gear support 802.1X, WPA3, central management, timely patching, and no default backdoors? If procurement never specifies these, security becomes a matter of luck. This test reviews whether wireless acquisition includes security requirements.
items.rootCause: Procurement is driven by cost, coverage, and delivery time, and security requirements are simply not part of the specification. Without them, teams buy whatever is cheapest or fastest, inheriting whatever weaknesses it carries.
items.impact: Missing acquisition requirements lead to consumer-grade gear, WPA2-PSK-only devices, unmanaged APs, default backdoors, and unsupported firmware entering the environment — the root cause behind many other wireless findings.
items.realWorldContext: A striking number of wireless weaknesses trace back to a purchase decision made with no security criteria at all. Building requirements like WPA3, 802.1X, central management and vendor support into procurement is what mature programs do to stop these problems arriving in the first place.
stepsToIdentify: Request the wireless procurement/acquisition standard and any security requirements it contains.
Check whether requirements cover WPA3/802.1X support, central management, patch/support terms, and no default backdoors.
Compare recently acquired wireless gear against these criteria.
Identify gear that would not have passed a proper acquisition gate.
Assess whether vendor security posture is evaluated during selection.
Document the acquisition-control gap.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to review procurement documentation.
Review the acquisition process for explicit wireless security requirements.
Map recent purchases to the (missing) requirements.
Show at least one device that a proper requirement would have rejected.
Correlate the gap with concrete downstream findings (consumer gear, weak auth).
Recommend acquisition-stage security requirements.
