examplePayloads.command: show ap summary && show ap image all

examplePayloads.label: Check each model's security capability
examplePayloads.command: # map model -> supported auth (802.1X/WPA3), management, vendor support status

examplePayloads.label: Cross-check vendor support/EOL
examplePayloads.command: # review vendor lifecycle pages for each acquired model

examplePayloads.label: Compare to (missing) standard
examplePayloads.command: # document which purchases would fail a security-requirements gate

variants: Purchases with no requirement for 802.1X/WPA3 support.
No requirement for a maintained patch/support contract.
No vendor security-posture evaluation during selection.
No prohibition on default/backdoor accounts.
mitigation: Add wireless security requirements to procurement: WPA3/802.1X, central management, patch/support, no default backdoors.
Evaluate vendor security posture and advisory history during selection.
Maintain an approved-hardware list that meets the standard.
Require lifecycle/EOL commitments in purchase terms.
Gate acquisitions on the security requirements before purchase.
Review the standard periodically as threats evolve.
items.mitigationClientFacing: How secure your Wi-Fi is often comes down to what you bought — whether it supports modern security, central management, and ongoing updates. If none of that is required when purchasing, security is left to chance. The fix is to build clear security requirements into how you buy wireless equipment, keep a list of approved gear that meets them, and check vendors' security track record before choosing.

items.title: Third-Party-Managed Guest Wi-Fi with Unclear Security Ownership
items.prerequisites: Access to information about the third-party guest-Wi-Fi provider and the contract/SLA, plus the ability to test the guest network. Authorization to assess the outsourced wireless service.
items.whatItIs: Many organizations outsource guest Wi-Fi to a third party (a captive-portal SaaS or a managed-Wi-Fi provider). If the security responsibilities — isolation from internal networks, data handling, patching, monitoring — are not clearly owned in the contract, gaps appear that neither party addresses. This test checks the security of, and ownership over, outsourced wireless services.
items.rootCause: Outsourcing shifts operation but not always accountability. Without explicit contractual security requirements and a clear responsibility matrix, both parties assume the other is handling isolation, monitoring, and patching.
items.impact: Unclear ownership can leave guest Wi-Fi bridged toward internal systems, guest data mishandled by the provider, or the provider's equipment unpatched and unmonitored — all exploitable, with no one accountable for the fix.
items.realWorldContext: Managed guest-Wi-Fi and captive-portal providers have been the source of real data exposures when responsibility for isolation and guest-data handling fell between the organization and the vendor. 'Who owns wireless security?' answered with a shrug is a recurring root cause behind outsourced-Wi-Fi findings.
stepsToIdentify: Identify whether guest wireless is provided/managed by a third party.
Review the contract/SLA for security responsibilities: isolation, data handling, patching, monitoring.
Test whether the guest network is truly isolated from internal systems.

items.title: Untrusted Supply Chain for Wireless Hardware / Firmware
items.prerequisites: Ability to verify AP hardware/firmware provenance and integrity (firmware hashes, vendor signatures) and authorization to inspect devices. Vendor firmware references.
items.whatItIs: Wireless hardware sourced from unverified channels — grey-market resellers, counterfeit units, or firmware from unofficial sources — can arrive with tampered firmware, hidden accounts, or implants. Without provenance and integrity checks, malicious wireless infrastructure can be deployed unknowingly. This test checks supply-chain integrity for wireless devices.
items.rootCause: Cost and availability pressures drive purchases through unofficial channels, and organizations rarely verify firmware signatures or hardware authenticity. Supply-chain integrity is assumed rather than checked.
items.impact: Tampered wireless firmware can include backdoors, capture traffic, or persist through resets — giving an attacker durable, trusted-looking infrastructure inside the network that is very hard to detect.
items.realWorldContext: Supply-chain implants and counterfeit networking gear are a documented national-security and enterprise concern, and firmware from unofficial sources has repeatedly been found trojanized. For wireless, a tampered AP is an attacker sitting permanently inside your walls, wearing a legitimate uniform.
stepsToIdentify: Identify the sourcing channel for wireless hardware and firmware.
Verify hardware authenticity (serials against vendor, anti-counterfeit features).
Verify firmware integrity against vendor-published hashes/signatures.
Check for unexpected accounts, services, or outbound connections on deployed APs.
Assess whether secure-boot / signed-firmware enforcement is enabled.
Document provenance and integrity verification gaps.
exploitationSteps: Confirm authorization to inspect wireless devices and firmware.
Validate serials/authenticity with the vendor where possible.
Extract running firmware and compare its hash/signature to the vendor's published values.
Inspect for unexpected accounts, listeners, or outbound beaconing.
Test whether unsigned/modified firmware can be loaded (secure-boot check).
Document any integrity failure and the supply-chain gap behind it.

mitigation: Source wireless hardware and firmware only through authorized channels.
Verify hardware authenticity and firmware signatures/hashes before deployment.
Enforce secure boot and signed-firmware where supported.
Monitor APs for unexpected accounts, services, and outbound connections.
Include supply-chain integrity requirements in procurement (SA-12).
Maintain provenance records for wireless assets.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Wi-Fi equipment bought from unofficial sources can arrive already tampered with — carrying hidden accounts or spy software that survives resets — turning a legitimate-looking access point into an attacker permanently inside your network. The fix is to buy wireless gear only through official channels, check that the hardware is genuine and the firmware is the vendor's untampered version, and monitor access points for unexpected behaviour.

items.title: Unpatched Access Point Firmware with Known CVEs
items.prerequisites: Ability to identify AP firmware versions and authorization to assess/validate known vulnerabilities. Vendor advisory and CVE references.
items.whatItIs: Access points run firmware that, like any software, has security bugs. Vendors publish patches, but APs are often left on old firmware for years. This test checks whether AP firmware is kept patched, by identifying versions in use and the known vulnerabilities they carry.
items.rootCause: APs are treated as appliances and patched rarely, if at all. There is often no firmware-update process, no tracking of advisories, and a fear that updates cause outages, so known-vulnerable firmware persists.
items.impact: Known AP firmware flaws include management-interface RCE, authentication bypass, and Wi-Fi protocol flaws (KRACK, FragAttacks-class). An attacker can exploit these for a foothold, persistence, or client compromise, using public exploit code.
items.realWorldContext: Edge devices like APs are prime targets precisely because their firmware is rarely updated, and public exploits for wireless management interfaces are readily available. Widespread flaws such as KRACK and the FragAttacks set showed how long known wireless bugs linger unpatched across real fleets.

Cross-reference each version against vendor advisories and public CVEs.
Identify APs missing security patches.
Prioritize by exploitability (remote, unauthenticated, public exploit available).
Check whether any firmware-update process/cadence exists.
Validate a high-impact known issue safely, in scope.

Match versions to known CVEs and patch availability.
For an in-scope, non-disruptive case, validate exploitability of a known management flaw.
Show the absence of a patch process behind the outdated firmware.

Track vendor advisories and CVEs for all deployed models.
Prioritize remotely-exploitable, unauthenticated issues.

Isolate un-patchable/EOL APs and plan replacement.
Feed firmware status into vulnerability management and metrics.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Access points run software that has security bugs, and vendors release fixes — but access points are often left on old, vulnerable versions for years, and ready-made attack tools exist for them. The fix is to set up a routine for updating access-point firmware, keep track of the vendor's security notices, patch the most dangerous issues first, and replace access points that can no longer be updated.

items.title: No Detection of Deauthentication / Disassociation Attacks
items.prerequisites: Wireless monitoring capability to review, and authorization to run a controlled deauth against a test client to check detection. Standard wireless tooling.
items.whatItIs: Deauthentication and disassociation frames can be forged to knock clients off Wi-Fi, force handshake captures, or push clients toward a rogue AP. On networks without management-frame protection or monitoring, these attacks are invisible. This test checks whether deauth/disassociation attacks are detected.
items.rootCause: Legacy Wi-Fi management frames are unauthenticated, so forged deauths are trivial. Without 802.11w and without wireless monitoring for deauth patterns, the attack leaves no trace in the defender's view.
items.impact: Undetected deauth attacks enable handshake capture (feeding PSK cracking), denial of service, and forced roaming to evil-twins — all foundational to other wireless attacks, and all silent without detection.
items.realWorldContext: Deauth is the opening move of most Wi-Fi attacks: force a reconnect, grab the handshake, crack offline — or repeat it to deny service. Yet most networks have no way to see a deauth flood at all, which is exactly why assessors use it freely during engagements.

Review whether any monitoring detects deauth/disassociation floods.
With authorization, run a short controlled deauth against a test client.
Observe whether any alert is generated.
Assess whether forced handshake capture would be detected.
Document detection gaps for management-frame attacks.

Baseline monitoring before testing.
Emit a brief, targeted deauth and confirm the client disconnects.
Capture the resulting handshake to show the downstream risk.
Check whether any WIDS/SIEM alert fired for the deauth or the capture.
Document the absence of detection and of 802.11w.

mitigation: Enable 802.11w (protected management frames) to reject forged deauths.
Deploy WIDS/WIPS to detect deauth/disassociation floods and alert.
Integrate wireless alerts into the SIEM and IR process.
Prefer WPA3, which mandates PMF.
Alert on abnormal client disconnect rates.
Test detection periodically with controlled events.
items.mitigationClientFacing: Attackers can send fake 'disconnect' messages to knock devices off Wi-Fi — to disrupt service, capture the data needed to crack the password, or push devices onto a fake network — and most networks never notice. The fix is to turn on the Wi-Fi feature that rejects fake disconnect messages, deploy wireless monitoring that spots these floods, and connect its alerts to your security team.

items.title: No Detection of Rogue AP / Evil-Twin Injection
items.prerequisites: Authorization to broadcast a benign test rogue/evil-twin SSID and observe detection. Wireless AP tooling (hostapd-mana, eaphammer).
items.whatItIs: An evil-twin is a rogue AP broadcasting a legitimate SSID to lure clients into connecting to the attacker instead of the real network. Without wireless monitoring that detects duplicate identities and unauthorized APs, evil-twins operate undetected. This test checks whether rogue-AP and evil-twin injection is detected.
items.rootCause: Clients trust SSIDs by name, and the network has no built-in way to notice another AP claiming its identity. Without WIDS correlating BSSIDs, signal, and authorized-AP lists, a rogue looks like just another AP.
items.impact: An undetected evil-twin harvests credentials (especially on WPA2-Enterprise with weak validation), intercepts traffic, and serves phishing portals — a full adversary-in-the-middle position that monitoring should catch but doesn't.
items.realWorldContext: Evil-twin attacks are a staple of both real intrusions and red-team engagements, and tools like eaphammer make credential-harvesting evil-twins trivial to stand up. Where there is no rogue-AP detection, the attack is invisible to the defender for as long as it runs.

Review whether same-SSID/different-BSSID events generate alerts.
With authorization, broadcast a benign test evil-twin of an in-scope SSID.
Observe whether it is detected and how quickly.
Assess whether clients would validate the server certificate on WPA2-Enterprise (mis-association risk).
Document detection gaps for rogue/evil-twin APs.

Baseline the wireless monitoring view.
Stand up a test evil-twin with the target SSID (clearly labelled, no real client capture).

Document the absence of detection and any mis-association exposure.

Without wireless monitoring that notices an impostor using your network's name, this runs undetected while it steals logins and traffic. The fix is to deploy wireless monitoring that keeps a list of your real access points and alerts on impostors, make devices verify they're talking to the genuine network, and use the latest Wi-Fi security.

items.title: Malicious or Modified Firmware Loadable onto APs
items.prerequisites: Access to the AP firmware-update mechanism and authorization to attempt loading a modified/unsigned image in a lab unit. Vendor firmware and signing references.
items.whatItIs: If an AP accepts firmware that is not cryptographically signed by the vendor, an attacker who reaches the update mechanism can load malicious firmware — adding backdoors, capturing traffic, or persisting through resets. This test checks whether firmware integrity is enforced on wireless devices.
items.rootCause: Some APs (especially consumer/older models) do not verify firmware signatures, or allow signed-firmware enforcement to be disabled. The update path then trusts whatever image it is given.
items.impact: Malicious firmware gives an attacker durable, trusted-looking control of the AP: traffic capture, backdoor access, and persistence that survives factory resets — extremely hard to detect or remove.
items.realWorldContext: Custom and trojanized firmware for consumer wireless gear is widespread, and the same lack of signature enforcement that enables hobbyist flashing enables malicious flashing. A backdoored AP that survives resets is a persistence dream for an attacker and a nightmare for defenders.

items.mitigationClientFacing: If an access point will accept software that isn't officially signed by the manufacturer, an attacker who reaches the update function can install malicious software that spies on traffic and survives even a factory reset. The fix is to use access points that only accept the manufacturer's genuine, signed firmware, prevent that protection from being switched off, lock down who can update them, and retire devices that can't enforce this.

items.title: No Integrity Monitoring of AP Configuration Drift
items.prerequisites: Access to AP/controller configuration and authorization to review change-monitoring. A known-good configuration baseline for comparison.
items.whatItIs: An AP's configuration can be changed — by an attacker who gains management access, or by accident — to weaken security: disabling PMF, enabling WPS, adding an SSID, or changing RADIUS settings. Without monitoring for configuration drift from a known-good baseline, such changes go unnoticed. This test checks whether AP configuration integrity is monitored.
items.rootCause: APs are configured once and rarely re-checked. There is often no baseline, no change detection, and no alerting, so a malicious or accidental configuration change simply becomes the new normal.
items.impact: Undetected configuration changes can silently disable protections (PMF, isolation), add rogue SSIDs, or redirect authentication — persisting until an incident forces a review. Attackers use exactly such changes to weaken defences quietly.
items.realWorldContext: Attackers who gain controller access frequently make small, quiet configuration changes — disabling a protection here, adding an SSID there — rather than anything loud. Without configuration-drift monitoring, these persist indefinitely, which is why baseline-and-alert is a hallmark of mature wireless operations.

items.mitigationClientFacing: An attacker who gets into your Wi-Fi management can quietly weaken it — turning off protections, adding a hidden network, or redirecting logins — and if nothing watches for changes, it goes unnoticed. The fix is to keep a record of the correct, secure settings, automatically compare against it and alert on any change, and restrict and log who can change wireless settings.

items.title: No Logging of Wireless Authentication Events
items.prerequisites: Access to review wireless authentication logging (controller/RADIUS logs) or its absence, and authorization for the review. A test client to generate auth events.
items.whatItIs: Wireless authentication events — successful and failed 802.1X/EAP or PSK associations — reveal who connected, when, and failed attempts that may indicate attacks. items.rootCause: Wireless auth logging requires controller/RADIUS log capture that is often not configured or centralized. Association events are ephemeral and, unlogged, leave no accountability trail.
items.impact: Without wireless auth logs, an attacker's association attempts, credential-stuffing against WPA2-Enterprise, and successful rogue connections go unrecorded, defeating detection and investigation of wireless access.
items.realWorldContext: When a wireless intrusion is investigated, the association and RADIUS auth logs are the primary evidence of who connected and of brute-force attempts — and their absence repeatedly leaves responders blind to how an attacker got onto the wireless network. Logging wireless authentication is basic accountability for the wireless edge.

The fix is to log all controller configuration changes with the person's identity, keep a history to compare against, and alert when security-sensitive wireless settings are changed.

items.prerequisites: Access to review wireless association-history retention (or its absence), and authorization for the review.
items.whatItIs: A history of which clients associated to which APs, and when, supports investigations (tracing a compromised device's movements) and anomaly detection. If association history is not retained, past wireless activity cannot be reconstructed. This tests whether wireless client association history is retained for a useful period.
items.rootCause: Association data is high-volume and treated as operational telemetry, so it is not retained or is purged quickly. Without retention, historical wireless activity is unavailable when needed.
items.impact: Without retained association history, responders cannot trace a compromised or rogue device's past presence and movement, and anomaly detection has no baseline — weakening both investigation and detection.
items.realWorldContext: Investigations into a compromised or rogue wireless device often need to answer 'where and when was it connected?' — and without retained association history, that question is unanswerable. Retaining association data for a useful window is what makes wireless investigation and anomaly detection possible.

items.mitigationClientFacing: A record of which devices connected to which access points, and when, helps you trace a compromised or rogue device later — but if this history isn't kept, that past activity is lost. The fix is to retain wireless connection history for a useful period, keep it searchable in one place, and use it for both investigations and spotting unusual behaviour.
